grammar.title: Nouns
grammar.html:
You have learnt that a noun is a word that names a person, place, animal, action, thing, quality or feeling.

Kinds of Nouns
Nouns are usually classified into four kinds.

  • A proper noun denotes a particular person, place or thing. For example, Italy, Mount Everest, Mohit, Taj Mahal.
  • A common noun denotes a person, place or thing in general. For example, city, mountain, boy, monument.
  • A collective noun denotes a collection of people, animals or things. For example, army, herd, bunch.
  • An abstract noun denotes a quality, an action or a state of being. For example, wisdom, honesty, wickedness.

There is a fifth kind of noun which names the material of which things are made.

A material noun denotes the matter or substance of which things are made. For example, jute, copper, paper.

NOTE:
Proper nouns, collective nouns, abstract nouns and material nouns can also be used as common nouns. They are then used in the plural number or have an article placed before them.

  • Mother Teresa served the poor of India. (proper noun)
    • She is the Mother Teresa of my country. (common noun)
  • Death is a great leveller. (abstract noun)
    • The media reported many deaths. (common noun)

A. Pick out the nouns in the passage and classify them. Place the nouns under the categories given below.
I visited Nainital when I was eight years old. We put up at a hotel by the lake. The beauty of the surrounding hills left a lasting impression on me. I distinctly remember the tiny boats that used to ply tourists and the shops selling delicious pastries. The Indian army had a camp nearby and every evening, officers in smart uniforms could be seen strolling about.
Every evening, young ladies draped in saris from Kancheepuram and children wrapped in woollens would come and sit on the benches that lined the lakeside. A batch of students from a nearby residential college was often spotted. My mother purchased a bangle from a silversmith and a few bronze statuettes. The kindness of the local people and the beauty of nature made the trip to Nainital memorable.

Proper Common Collective Abstract Material

You have learnt that abstract nouns can be formed from adjectives and verbs as well as from common nouns by adding suffixes. For example,

  • sweet—sweetness (from an adjective)
  • move—movement (from a verb)
  • boy—boyhood (from a common noun)

NOTE:
Some other suffixes that are used to form abstract nouns are -sion, -al, -ship, -dom, -th, -tion and -cy.

You know that a collective noun is used to denote several persons or things regarded as one group. Sometimes, collective nouns can be considered as singular or plural, depending on the context. For example,

  • The jury agrees that the accused is guilty. (Jury acts as a unit here.)
  • The jury disagree that the accused is guilty. (Jury acts as a unit, but the people in the jury are acting as individuals.)

D. Fill in the blanks with suitable collective nouns. Choose from those provided within brackets.

  1. An ____ of poems by Rilke is on display. (library, anthology, auction)
  2. A ____ of policemen entered the premises. (panel, posse, band)
  3. The ____ sang beautifully during the Sunday mass at the Church. (company, coterie, choir)
  4. The ____ were unwilling to leave port as the ship needed repairs. (captain, crew, convoy)
  5. The ____ waited expectantly for the performer to arrive. (society, audience, horde)
  6. The ____ of trees at that corner will have to be cut down. (clutch, clump, truss)
  7. The ____ gave its verdict and the criminal was sent to jail. (judge, jury, board)
  8. A ____ of musicians arrived for the show. (band, troop, soiree)
  9. A ____ of robbers attacked them on the highway. (group, gang, galaxy)
  10. Place the ____ of eggs in this basket. (cluster, clutch, brood)

Gender

Nouns may be in the masculine, feminine, neuter or common gender.

A noun is said to be in the masculine gender if it refers to a male. For example, man, tiger, uncle.

A noun is said to be in the feminine gender if it refers to a female. For example, woman, tigress, aunt.

A noun is said to be in the neuter gender if it refers to things that are neither male nor female. Nouns referring to non-living things are of the neuter gender. For example, stone, grass, sand.

A noun is said to be in the common gender if what it refers to can be a male or a female. For example, student, orphan, baby.

NOTE:
Objects associated with strength and power are sometimes regarded as male. For example, Sun, Death. Objects associated with beauty and gentleness are usually regarded as female. For example, Nature, Earth.

  10. The hero of the film walked up to the director, who was sitting on the grass, and said that he needed to meet a friend.

Number
In English, a noun may either be singular or plural in number.

When we speak about one person, one animal or one thing, we use the noun in the singular form. For example, boy, tiger, box.

When we speak about two or more people, animals or things, we use the noun in the plural form. For example, boys, tigers, boxes.

Singular nouns can be changed to plural in various ways. Look at this table and revise the rules that you have studied before.

Rule Singular Plural
By adding -s to the singular form garden, stone gardens, stones
By adding -es to nouns ending in -x, -ch, -s, -sh tax, watch, gas, dish taxes, watches, gases, dishes
In nouns ending in -y, by changing -y into -i and adding -es duty, story duties, stories
In nouns ending in -y but preceded by a vowel, by adding s day, monkey days, monkeys
In nouns ending in -o preceded by a consonant, by adding -es mosquito, volcano, hero, buffalo mosquitoes, volcanoes, heroes, buffaloes
In nouns ending in -ie, -oo or -eo and in some words ending in -o preceded by a consonant, by adding -s tie, cuckoo, video, piano ties, cuckoos, videos, pianos
In nouns ending in -f or -fe, by changing -f or -fe into -v and adding -es calf, knife calves, knives
In some nouns ending in -f, by adding -s gulf, roof, cliff gulfs, roofs, cliffs
Some nouns do not follow any of the above rules hoof, dwarf hoofs/hooves, dwarfs/dwarves
Some nouns have the same singular and plural forms bison, deer, moose, aircraft bison, deer, moose, aircraft

  3. The ____ (child) as well as the ____ (woman) of the ____ (colony) walked to the mayor's office.
  4. The ____ (deer) ran into the forest as they were being chased by ____ (wolf).
  5. The ____ (goose) wandered into the ____ (pond) where some ____ (calf) were bathing.
  6. The ____ (elf) stitched the ____ (shoe) in record time.
  7. The ____ (footman) ran down the ____ (stair) to stop the ____ (carriage).

Now, read some more rules.

  • Compound nouns generally form their plurals by adding -s to the main noun. For example,

    • father-in-law—fathers-in-law
    • step-daughter—stepdaughters

  • Some words are generally used in the singular form. For example, poetry, information, furniture, scenery, mathematics, politics, advice, machinery, alms, innings.

  • Nouns that describe things having two similar parts are considered to be plural nouns. For example, jeans, glasses, tongs, socks, trousers, scissors.

  • Some nouns denoting a specific quantity or amount are considered to be singular. For example, three dozen apples, two hundred miles.

  • Some words in the English language have been borrowed from Latin. Some nouns of Latin origin that end in -us form their plurals by adding -es. For example, circuses, campuses, viruses.

grammar.title: Pronouns
grammar.html:
You have learnt that words that take the place of nouns are called pronouns.

Pronouns are of different kinds.

  • personal pronouns
  • possessive pronouns
  • demonstrative pronouns
  • interrogative pronouns
  • reflexive pronouns
  • emphasising pronouns
  • indefinite pronouns
  • distributive pronouns
  • relative pronouns

Read this sentence.

  • Mohit is an athlete. He practises regularly. The coach likes him.
    In the above sentence, he and him take the place of Mohit. These pronouns take the place of persons or things.

Pronouns that take the place of people and things are called personal pronouns.

We use personal pronouns depending upon—

  • number—singular or plural. For example,
    • The children went to a party. They enjoyed it.
  • gender—male, female or neuter. For example,
    • Mahima is in the pool. She loves swimming.
    • Tanish is a good boy. He always obeys his parents.
  • person—first person, second person or third person. For example,
    • I told you not to tell her the secret.
    • They agreed to meet us at 8 a.m.
  • case—subject or object. For example,
    • Gaurav is a good student. He is also good in sports.
    • Jayant gave me the book.

NOTE:
The pronoun, it is used—

  • for non-living things. For example,
    • Here is your knife. Keep it carefully.
  • to refer to an earlier statement. For example,
    • He must leave. He knows it.
  • to emphasise a noun or pronoun that follows it. For example,
  • It was I who promised to help you.

Now, read these sentences. 

- This chair is mine.
- Those books are theirs.

The highlighted pronouns show possession or belonging.

Pronouns that show possession are known as possessive pronouns.

Now, read these sentences.

  • This is a beautiful dress.
  • Those are ripe mangoes.

Pronouns like this, that, those and these are used to point out certain objects.

Pronouns that are used to point out the objects which they refer to are known as demonstrative pronouns.

Now, read these sentences.

  • What would you like to have—tea or coffee?
  • Which is the way to the university?

Pronouns like what, who and which are used to ask questions.

Pronouns that are used to ask questions are called interrogative pronouns.

NOTE:
This and these are used to refer to things that are close by. That and those are used to refer to things that are far away.

NOTE:
Who is used to refer to persons. Which is used to refer to persons or things. What is used only for things.

Read this sentence.

  • He hurt himself.
  • The cat licked itself.

The highlighted pronouns tell us that the subject is the receiver of the action.

The highlighted pronouns are called reflexive pronouns because the action of the subject reflects upon the subject itself.

NOTE:
The reflexive pronoun is used when the subject and the object of the verb refer to the same person or thing.
A reflexive pronoun can never be the subject of a sentence.

  • My sister and myself went to Kolkata. (incorrect)
  • My sister and I went to Kolkata. (correct)

Now, read these sentences.

  • He himself should finish the work.
  • I myself closed the door.
    The highlighted pronouns are used for emphasis.

Pronouns that are used for the sake of emphasis are called emphasising pronouns.

A. Fill in the blanks with pronouns that refer to the highlighted word/group of words.

  2. Did you do the homework yourself/herself/ourselves?

  4. I cut my hair ourselves/myself/themselves.
  5. She looked at itself/herself/themselves in the mirror.
  6. You express himself/herself/yourself very well.
  7. They themselves/ourselves/yourself started the fight first.
  8. Roshni doesn't care about anyone. She only thinks about himself/herself/themselves.

Now, read these sentences.

  • Somebody has left the door open.
  • Few escaped punishment that morning.
    These highlighted pronouns do not refer to any specific person or thing.

Pronouns that refer to some person or thing in a general way and do not refer to any person in particular are called indefinite pronouns.

The other indefinite pronouns are—all, another, any, anybody, anyone, anything, each, everybody, everyone, everything, few, many, nobody, none, one, several, some, somebody, someone.

NOTE:
The indefinite pronoun one, if used in a sentence should be used throughout.

  • One must never abandon one's duties.

C. There are errors in each of these sentences. Rewrite the sentences correctly.

  2. I am shorter than him.
  3. Which is the news that you bring?
  4. It was him who should have protested.
  5. I and Ram have been chosen to lead the team.
  6. Which is the purpose of this plan?
  7. She and me are to blame for this mess.
  8. The members of the jury was divided in its opinion.
  9. Between you and I, there is no truth in this.
  10. One must be careful about what he says.
  11. Anybody was there to save the drowning child.
  12. My uncle asked my sister and I to accompany him.
  13. My aunt and myself decided to see a film.
  14. Any of the children are ready to participate in the programme tomorrow.
  15. Our players were better prepared than that of China.

Now, read these sentences.

  • Each of us must contribute generously.
  • Either of you can take down the notes.
  • Neither of them attended the ceremony.
  • Either of the two students may be sent to the competition.
  • Neither of the coats is suitable for the occasion.

NOTE:
Either and neither can be used only when speaking about two persons or things. Either means one or the other of two. Neither means not one nor the other of two.

The pronouns each, either and neither refer to persons or things one at a time.
Pronouns that refer to nouns one at a time are called distributive pronouns.
Distributive pronouns are always in the singular and take singular verbs.

Now, read this sentence.

  • The boy who you were talking to is the captain of the cricket team.

In this sentence, who is a relative pronoun that refers to the noun boy that comes before. The noun is thus the antecedent of the pronoun. The relative pronoun should ideally be placed close to its antecedent in the sentence.

NOTE:
Generally, who is used while referring to people, which for non-living things or animals and that is used for people and things. As the relative pronoun refers to a noun or a pronoun, it must be of the same number and person as its antecedent. It is the verb that shows the number and person of the relative pronoun.
Sometimes the relative pronoun is omitted. For example,

  • This is the house (that) my grandfather built.

grammar.title: Adjectives
grammar.html:
Words that are used to describe a noun or a pronoun are called adjectives. Adjectives help us to know more about nouns and pronouns by expressing their qualities.

Kinds of Adjectives
There are six kinds of adjectives. They are—

  • adjectives of quality
  • adjectives of quantity
  • adjectives of number
  • demonstrative adjectives
  • interrogative adjectives
  • emphasising adjectives

Read these sentences.

  • He is a brave soldier.
  • Mana is a kind girl.

The highlighted adjectives tell us what kind of noun is being spoken about.

Adjectives of quality express the kind or quality of a person or a thing.

Now, read these sentences.

  • I need some money to buy stationery.
  • There is not much ink in the bottle.

The highlighted adjectives tell us what kind how much of a thing is meant.

Adjectives of quantity tell us how much of a thing is meant.

Look at these sentences.

  • This box contains ten apples.
  • Today is the last day of the festival.
    The highlighted adjectives answer the question how many or in what order.

Adjectives of number tell us how many people or things are meant or in what order a person or a thing stands.

Adjectives of number are of three kinds.

  • Definite numeral adjectives tell us the exact number of people or things. They are of two kinds—
    • cardinals state the number of people or things. For example, forty thieves, twenty-five years.
    • ordinals give the order of people or things in a series. For example, first man on the moon, last day of the week.
  • Indefinite numeral adjectives do not indicate the exact number. For example, few children, many people.
  • Distributive numeral adjectives refer to each one of a number.
    • Every person must attend the meeting.
    • Each girl should participate in the competition.

NOTE:
Some adjectives can be classified as adjectives of number as well as adjectives of quantity depending on their usage in a sentence. Look at the examples given below.

Adjective of quantity Adjective of number
He has lost all his money. All participants must submit a letter.
He did not drink any water. Are there any charts in the book?

Look at these sentences.

  • This book is expensive.
  • These apples are from Himachal Pradesh.

Demonstrative adjectives point out which person or thing is meant.

Now, read these sentences.

  • Which pen do you want to buy?
  • Whose house is that?
    The highlighted adjectives are used to ask questions about the nouns that follow them.

Words like what, which and whose when used with nouns to ask questions are called interrogative adjectives.

Take a look at these sentences.

  • The campaign was a complete success.
  • This is the very dress that I wanted to buy.
    The highlighted adjectives are used to lay emphasis on the nouns that follow.

The adjectives that we use to emphasise what we want to say are called emphasising adjectives.

NOTE:

  • Some and any are used in affirmative and negative sentences, respectively. For example,
    • I have bought some pens.
    • I have not purchased any pens.
  • Little is used with uncountable nouns and few with countable nouns. For example,
    • There is little hope of recovery.
    • There were a few chairs scattered around the room.
  • Few means not many, while a few means some. For example,
    • Sometimes, a few birds perch on this tree.
    • Few students were at school today.
  • Older and oldest indicate age and are used to compare people or things. Elder and eldest are used with reference to family members. For example,
    • My eldest brother will arrive today.
    • Jagriti is older than Mahesh.
    • This is the oldest house in the colony.
  • Later and latest denote time and latter and last denote position.
    • I am rather busy now and will see you later.
    • Which is the latest magazine?
    • Go and sit on the last bench.
    • Jaya and Rajeev are both good swimmers, but the latter is a more sporting loser.
  • Nearest denotes distance and next denotes position.
    • How far is the nearest bus stop?
    • Sita's house is next to mine.

  2. I like ____ sweets. (Turk/Turkish)

  5. ____ citizen must vote. (all/every)
  6. Bring me ____ chair. (these/that)

  13. What is the ____ news? (later/latest)
  14. You can take ____ of the four toys. (either/one)

Participal Adjectives

Look at these sentences.

  • We stood in front of a running stream.
  • We heard the interesting news.
    The highlighted words are present participles (verb + -ing form).

Now, read these sentences.

  • People say that this is a haunted house.
  • The burnt cottage was razed to the ground.
    The highlighted words are past participles (verb + -ed/-t/-n form).

You will notice that in these sentences, the present participles and the past participles have been used as adjectives.

Present participles and past participles, when used as adjectives, are called participial adjectives.

B. Underline the adjectives in this paragraph. Identify the participial adjectives.
I reached the forbidding building on Park Avenue in a black car. I knocked on the closed door and a short bald man opened the door. I entered a bright room lit with glowing candles. By the fireplace, there was a big easy chair with a shining tea table and a smaller chair beside it. A girl in a pretty dress and a cheerful smile appeared from nowhere. I felt shy. On the other side of the barred window, the glorious sun was setting the evening sky aflame. Suddenly, I noticed a sombre man sitting on an upholstered divan with a Persian rug over his knees. Behind him was a spectacular painting by Van Gogh. The crimson flowers and the golden cornfields had been painted with passion. I was impressed by the interesting décor of the room. However, the reigning silence was somewhat disturbing.

  21. The kitten was playing with the falling leaves.
  22. The police caught the prisoner who had escaped.
  23. It was such a long and boring flight.
  24. I am very frightened of lizards.
  25. What a frightening film!

Degrees of Comparison

You have learnt that adjectives have three degrees of comparison—positive, comparative and superlative. Let us revise what we know.

Read these sentences.

  • This is a good violin.
  • My violin is better than the one you bought.
  • Bobby's violin is the best of all our violins.

The adjective good is used when we talk about one person or thing. It is said to be in the positive degree.

The positive degree is used when no comparison is made.

The adjective better is used to compare two things. It conveys a higher degree of quality than that of the positive. The adjective better is said to be in the comparative degree.

The comparative degree is used to compare two people or things.

The adjective best is used to compare more than two things. The adjective best is said to be in the superlative degree.

The superlative degree can be used to compare more than two things. It denotes the highest degree of quality.

NOTE:
When we use the comparative degree, we always use the word than to compare and contrast two things.
The superlative degree, on the other hand, is always preceded by the word the.

grammar.title: Adverbs
grammar.html:
You have learnt that an adverb is a word which modifies the meaning of a verb, an adjective or another adverb.

Kinds of Adverbs

There are six kinds of adverbs.

Adverbs of time show us the time at which an action takes place.

For example,

  • I have met Neha before.
  • The principal will meet you today.

Adverbs of frequency show us how often something happens.

For example,

  • He visits us regularly.
  • My father exercises every day.

Adverbs of place show us where something happens.

For example,

  • Sam went downstairs.
  • The man has gone out.

Adverbs of manner show us how something happens.

For example,

  • Rahim writes neatly.
  • The students worked diligently.

NOTE:
Sometimes, an adverb can modify an entire sentence. For example,

  • Luckily, she was not seriously injured.

Adverbs of degree show the intensity or the degree of an action or a quality.

For example,

  • I am so satisfied!
  • What you have heard is absolutely true.

Interrogative adverbs are adverbs which are used at the beginning of a sentence to ask questions.

For example,

  • When are you reaching Kolkata? (time)
  • Where can I meet you? (place)
  • How did you get here? (manner)
  • Why are you sad? (reason)

A. Fill in the blanks with the kind of adverbs mentioned in the brackets.

  1. She arrived ____ for the class. (adverb of time)
  2. This mango is ____ ripe. (adverb of degree)
  3. We walked ____ in the direction of the school. (adverb of manner)
  4. The grains were scattered ____. (adverb of place)
  5. She will return ____ from Delhi. (adverb of time)
  6. I cannot read the notes. He writes ____. (adverb of manner)
  7. The child wept ____. (adverb of manner)
  8. Rajiv ____ spoke ill of others. (adverb of frequency)
  9. Breakfast is ____ ready. (adverb of degree)
  10. He ____ visits us in May. (adverb of frequency)
  11. He will get a job ____. (adverb of place)
  12. She ____ travels by bus. (adverb of frequency)
  13. ____ do you usually come home? (interrogative adverb of time)
  14. She is ____ ill to go to work. (adverb of degree)
  15. The father looked ____ at the baby. (adverb of manner)

Formation of Adverbs
Most adverbs of manner are formed from adjectives in the following ways.

  • Most adjectives can be changed to adverbs by adding -ly. For example, warm—warmly, sincere—sincerely, quiet—quietly.
  • When the adjective ends in -y preceded by a consonant, -y is changed to -i and -ly is added. For example, pretty—prettily, steady—steadily, lucky—luckily.
  • When the adjective ends in -le, the -le is changed to -ly. For example, possible—possibly, able—ably, gentle—gently.
  • When the adjective ends in -ic, we add -ally. For example, basic—basically, scientific—scientifically.

NOTE:
Some adverbs and adjectives have the same form, but are used differently.

  • We need fast bowlers. (adjective)
  • He bowls fast. (adverb)
  • We must be quick. (adverb)
  • The smart child gave a quick reply. (adjective)

B. State whether the highlighted words are adverbs or adjectives.

  1. The teacher dictated the notes in a loud voice.
  2. There is enough milk in the pot.
  3. He visits his mother daily.
  4. I have worked enough for a day.
  5. The early riser enjoys a longer day!
  6. Work hard if you wish to do well.
  7. The politician spoke loudly.
  8. Exercise should be a part of your daily routine.
  9. Late arrivals were sent back home.
  10. He arrived early.
  11. The children sang merrily.
  12. He reached the station late.
  13. This truly is a hard nut!
  14. This will be a long wait.
  15. She hit him hard.

Position of Adverbs

  • Adverbs of manner, which answer the question How?, are generally placed after the verb. If the verb has a direct object, then the adverb is placed after the direct object. For example,
    • The actor is singing loudly.
    • He plays the flute well.

NOTE:

  • The direct object is the person or thing that receives the action of the verb. The direct object follows the verb. We can identify the direct object by asking the question Whom? or What? after the verb. For example:
  • The boy recited a poem. (What did the boy recite?)

  • Sudha is biting her nails. (What is Sudha biting?)

  • Adverbs of place and adverbs of time are also placed after the verb. If the sentence has a direct object, then the adverb is placed after the direct object. For example:

    • It snowed yesterday.
    • Put the chairs there.

  • When there are two or more adverbs after a verb, the normal order is adverb of manner followed by adverb of place and then adverb of time.

    • Rima will come here next month.

  • Adverbs of frequency, adverbs of degree and sometimes adverbs of manner are normally put between the subject and the verb if the verb consists of only one word. For example:

    • I quite like these shoes.
    • I always tell him to exercise.
    • She happily accepted the suggestion.

NOTE:

  • If the verb consists of more than one word, then the adverb comes after the first verb. For example:
    • The man had just entered the auditorium.
  • If the verb is am/are/is/was, the adverbs are placed after the verb. For example:
    • They are always late.
    • The rice is just right.
  • When an adverb modifies an adjective or another adverb, the adverb usually comes before it. For example:
    • He lifted the stone quite easily.
    • It is a rather warm day.
  • The adverb enough is always placed after the word which it modifies. For example:
    • Is this good enough for you?
    • Is the box large enough for all your books?
  • The word only should be placed before the word it modifies. For example:
    • I only have four bags right now.
  • For emphasis, adverbs of time may also be placed at the beginning of the sentence. For example:
    • Tomorrow, we shall meet.

C. Insert the adverbs given in the brackets in their correct positions.

  1. I am often late for school. (often)
  2. Sam readily agreed to the plan. (readily)
  3. He has almost finished the work. (almost)
  4. He seldom disagrees with me. (seldom)
  5. She usually cycles to school. (usually)
  6. He did fairly well in the exam. (fairly)
  7. I only asked for a glass of milk. (only)
  8. We shall certainly meet you soon. (certainly)
  9. I rather like the book that I bought yesterday. (rather)
  10. He was brave enough to challenge the authorities. (enough)

Use of Simple Adverbs
NOTE: the use of these common adverbs.

  • Very is intensively used with an adjective or another adverb in the positive degree. For example,
    • He is a very nice person.
    • I typed very carefully.
  • Very with a superlative is used to indicate the highest degree. For example,
    • The coffee is of the very best quality.
    • I can reach by 7 a.m. at the very earliest.
  • Too is used to mean more than required or excess. For example,
    • I am too tired to play now.
    • It is too cold to go for a walk in the woods.
  • Much is used with an adverb or an adjective in the comparative degree. For example,
    • Things are much better in the city.
    • You are much stronger than I thought you would be.

NOTE:
We say, It is very hot today.
We do not say, It is too hot today.

We say, It is too hot to go cycling.
We do not say, It is very hot to go cycling.

D. Fill in the blanks with very, too or much as required.

  2. I am ____ glad to see you.
  3. Ishaan plays tennis ____ well.
  4. I am ____ sleepy to go for a jog tonight.
  5. Her handwriting is ____ worse than mine.
  6. The movie was ____ better than I expected.
  7. You have to be ____ careful when you go to the beach in the rainy season.
  8. The watch wasn't ____ expensive, so I bought it
  9. When we went to Goa, the weather was ____ nice.
  10. The eagle swooped upon the rabbit ____ quickly.
  11. It's _____ dark outside.
  12. That was a ____ good answer.

One Word for Several Words
We often use an adverb in place of a group of words. So adverbs are useful when we wish to express something concisely. For example,

  • I reminded Ravi again and again that he had to pick up his sister from school.
  • I reminded Ravi repeatedly that he had to pick up his sister from school.

grammar.title: Articles
grammar.html:
You have learnt that there are three articles—a, an and the.

Indefinite Articles
The articles a and an are called indefinite articles because they do not point to a particular person or thing. Let us look at the uses of the indefinite articles.

  • We use a and an before countable nouns in the singular number. For example,
    • a desk
    • an orange

NOTE:
We do not say a milk or a lemonade because they are uncountable nouns. However, we can say a cup of milk or a glass of lemonade.

  • We use a before words that begin with a consonant sound. We use an before words that begin with a vowel sound. For example,

    • a thirsty crow
    • a good friend
    • an empty bottle
    • an independent state

  • We use a before words that begin with e and u because they have an initial 'y' sound. For example,

    • a university
    • a European

  • We use a before words that begin with o but sound like 'w'. For example,

    • a one-storey building

  • We use an before words that begin with a silent h. For example,

    • an heir
    • an honest politician

  • We use an before abbreviations, if consonants begin with a vowel sound. For example,

    • an MA
    • an MP

  • We use a or an before a singular countable noun which is used to represent a class of things. For example,

    • A cow is a useful animal.

  • We use a or an to indicate one. For example,

    • Not a bird could be heard.

  • We use a or an to make a common noun of a proper noun. For example,

    • We have a Daniel in our midst!

  • We use a or an when we speak of a profession. For example,

    • He is a doctor.

  • We use a before words like dozen, quarter, thousand, few, little and lot of. For example,

    • Can you give me a little sugar?
    • He bought a few mangoes.
    • It is a quarter of a kilometre to the school.

A. Insert a/an where required.

  1. What ____ shame! He cannot make it to the reunion.
  2. He is ____ honourable man but has been largely misunderstood.
  3. I met ____ Assamese gentleman while travelling from Agra to ____ hill station.
  4. He has ____ headache and needs to take rest.
  5. The workers formed ____ union in order to discuss their problems.
  6. Can you give me ____ one-rupee note?
  7. ____ honest person will never lie.
  8. She wants to buy ____ South Indian saree.
  9. ____ aunt of mine, who lives in Egypt, will visit us in summer.
  10. Our train is late by ____ hour. We may have to change our plans.
  11. Could you add ____ little salt to the salad?
  12. I need ____ lot of money to fulfil my dreams.

Definite Articles
The is called the definite article because it points to a particular person or a specific thing. Let us learn the uses of the definite article.

We use the when we speak of a particular person or thing, or one that has already been referred to. For example,

  • A thirsty crow found a pitcher that contained some water. The clever crow picked up some pebbles in his beak and dropped them one by one into the pitcher.

We use the when a singular common noun is used to indicate a whole class. For example,

  • The lion is the king of the jungle.

We use the with superlatives. For example,

  • Sachin is one of the most popular sportsmen in the world.

We use the with objects that are unique. For example,

  • the sun
  • the moon

We use the before phrases like first, last, only, next, following and previous. For example,

  • She is sitting in the last row.

We use the before ordinals. For example,

  • Her examination starts on the third of March.

We use the when we speak of the population of a nation. For example,

  • The Japanese are warm-hearted people.

We use the before the names of trains, planes and ships. For example,

  • the Titanic
  • the Golden Temple Express

We use the before the names of well-known buildings and institutions. For example,

  • the Parliament House
  • the Red Fort

We use the before the names of newspapers and magazines. For example,

  • the Deccan Herald
  • the Hindu

We use the with adjectives, when we use them to refer to a whole group of people. For example,

  • We should help the poor. (poor people)

We use the with the names of rivers, seas, oceans, mountains and deserts. For example,

  • the Ganges
  • the Indian Ocean
  • the Arabian Sea
  • the Sahara Desert

We use the before points of the compass that are used as geographic areas. For example,

  • the Middle East
  • the West

We use the before points on the globe. For example,

  • the equator
  • the south pole

Omission of Articles
We do not use articles—

  • before expressions like last night, last week, last year, next week and next month.
  • before proper nouns. For example,
  • I am going to Australia.
  • Have you spoken to Hema?
  • before names of languages. For example,
  • They speak German quite well.
  • before plural countable nouns that refer to the entire class. For example,
  • I do not like bananas.
  • before material nouns. For example,
  • Platinum is an expensive metal.
  • before abstract nouns when used in a general way. For example,
  • Honesty is a virtue.
  • before the names of games and sports. For example,
  • Golf is gaining in popularity in India of late.
  • Rakesh loves playing hockey.
  • before the names of meals. For example,
  • I ate breakfast quite late today.
  • before expressions such as all day, all night, by air and by sea. For example,
  • The contingent for the Asian Games will travel by air.

NOTE:
In certain cases, there is a need to repeat an article to make the meaning clear. Look at these sentences carefully.

  • The Trustee and Secretary arrived.
  • The Trustee and the Secretary arrived.

The first sentence implies that only one person who was both Trustee and Secretary arrived.
The second sentence states that two persons arrived—the Trustee and the Secretary.

  2. Moon is shining in the sky.
  3. Don't play fool.
  4. This is a best of the lot!
  5. Kindness that he showed was truly touching.
  6. The privileged of community should help poor.
  7. I hope to be the actor.
  8. I met a Austrian at an university in the Germany.

grammar.title: Perfect Tenses
grammar.html:
The perfect tenses show that an action has already been completed. The word perfect means completed.

The present perfect tense tells us that an action is complete with respect to the present. For example,

  • I have seen this movie twice this week. (And the week isn't over yet.)

The past perfect tense tells us that an action took place before another action in the past. For example,

  • Mala had left before I reached the office.

The future perfect tense talks about an action that will occur in the future before some other action. For example,

  • I will have arrived before you come home.

Present Perfect Tense
The present perfect is used—

  • to indicate that an action has been completed just now or a little while ago. For example,
    • He has just finished correcting answer scripts.
    • The sun has risen a while ago.
  • to express an action whose time is not given and is not definite. For example,
    • We have known her to be very helpful.
  • to describe a past event when we think more about its effect on the present. For example,
    • I have broken my glasses. (So, I cannot see properly.)
  • to denote an action that started some time ago and is continuing till the time of speaking. For example,
    • We have known the family for many years.
    • Manju has been ill since Sunday.

NOTE:
Both the simple past tense and the present perfect tense express an action completed in the past. But the simple past tense expresses an action completed in the past, but not linked to the present. The present perfect tense, however, denotes an action that is completed but connected to the present.
The present perfect tense is never used with adverbs or phrases of past time like yesterday, last month, etc.
We do not say, He has gone to the museum yesterday.
We say, He went to the museum yesterday.

Past Perfect Tense
We use the past perfect tense to denote—

  • an action completed before a given point of time. This moment or point of time may be indicated or may be understood.
    • When I reached the station, the train had left.
    • I had completed my training by noon.

NOTE:
If two actions occurred in the past, with one action taking place earlier than the other, the past perfect is used for the earlier action and the simple past for the later action. Thus, we say,

  • The exam had started when I reached school.

The past perfect tense is used with such verbs as hope, expect, think to indicate that a past hope or desire remained unfulfilled.

  • I had believed that I would win the tournament but I did not.

Future Perfect Tense
The future perfect tense is used—

  • to refer to the completion of an action by a certain time in the future. The tense is normally used with a time expression beginning with by, such as, by that time, by then or by next week.
    • The Minister will have announced his decision by next week.
    • They will have completed the assignment by next summer.
    • The jury will have given its verdict by noon tomorrow.
    • By next week, we shall have reached an agreement regarding the factory.

grammar.title: Modals and Auxiliaries
grammar.html:
An auxiliary is a helping verb. In a sentence, an auxiliary is always used with another verb. There are two types of auxiliary verbs.

  • primary auxiliaries: The words be, have and do are called primary auxiliaries. The forms of be are is, am, are, was and were. The forms of have are have, has and had. The forms of do are do, does and did.
  • modal auxiliaries: The words can, could, may, might, shall, should, must, will, would, used, need, dare, ought express attitudes like permission, possibility, etc. Modal auxiliaries are also called modals. They do not change their forms.

Primary Auxiliaries

Be

  • It is used in the formation of continuous tenses. For example,
    • Mother is knitting a sweater.
  • It is used to show that the action is more important than the doer. For example,
    • The cupboard was opened by Kirti.
  • When followed by an infinitive, it is used to indicate a plan or an arrangement. For example,
    • We are to finish the work in a month.
  • It is also used to denote a command. For example,
    • You are to pick it up right now.

Have

  • This is used to form the perfect tenses. For example,
    • The artists have painted beautifully.
  • It is used with the infinitive to indicate some kind of obligation. For example,
    • They have to return immediately.

Do

  • It is used to form negative statements and interrogative sentences. For example,
  • He doesn't agree with me.
  • Did you manage to finish the assignment?
  • In imperative sentences, it is used to make the statement more forceful. For example,
  • Do be quiet.

Modal Auxiliaries

Can and Could

  • Can usually suggests potential or ability. For example,
    • Ram can take you to the airport.
    • Can you lift this?
  • Can is also used to indicate permission. For example,
    • You can join from tomorrow.
  • Could is used to ask a polite question. For example,
    • Could you help me solve the sum?
  • Could is used as the past tense of can in indirect speech. For example,
    • Toto said, 'I can help you.'
    • Toto said that he could help me.
  • Could is used to indicate ability in the past. For example,
    • He could sing well once upon a time.

May and Might

  • May is usually used to request permission formally. For example,
    • May I use your eraser?
  • May is also used to express a wish. For example,
    • May you always enjoy good luck!
  • May is used to indicate possibility. For example,
    • There may be some rain this evening.
  • May suggests a weak possibility and might suggests a very weak possibility in the future. For example,
    • The match schedule may be announced next Monday.
    • We might return sooner than expected.
    • She might arrive tomorrow.

Shall, Should, Will and Would

  • Shall is usually used in the first person and will in the second and third person. For example,
    • I shall be pleased to visit you.
    • You will agree with me.
  • Shall is used in the second and third person to express a command, a promise or even a threat. For example,
    • He shall not work here again. (threat)
    • You shall certainly be rewarded. (promise)
  • Shall is used in interrogative sentences with the first person to indicate an offer or a suggestion. For example,
    • Shall I carry these books for you?
  • Will is used to express a decision or a choice. For example,
    • I will do the cooking today.
  • Will is used to indicate a habit. For example,
    • He will go swimming as usual.
  • Will is used in interrogative sentences to suggest an invitation. For example,
    • Will you go on a holiday with us?
  • In clauses starting with if, should is used to express a supposition that may not be true. For example,
    • If it should rain, the match will be called off.

Must and Ought

  • Must expresses necessity or obligation. For example,
    • We must remember this.
  • Must can express fixed determination. For example,
    • I must have an opportunity to do what I wish.
  • Must and ought also express certainty or strong possibility. For example,
    • He must have forgotten about the invitation.
    • We ought to strike this deal.
  • Ought expresses moral obligation or desirability. For example,
    • We ought to try hard.

Used

  • It is used to indicate a discontinued habit. For example,
  • She used to learn ballet.

Need

  • It denotes necessity or obligation. It is commonly used in negatives and interrogatives. For example,
    • He need not give up tennis.
    • Need I help him?
  • Need can also be used to denote requirement or desire. For example,
    • I do not need your help.

Dare
Dare as modal auxiliary means 'be bold enough to'.

  • It is commonly used in interrogative and negative sentences.
    • How dare she say this?
  • Dare can also be used to indicate a challenge. For example,
    • I dare you to eat all the food on the table.

    • They are swimming.

In a sentence, the verb usually changes its form according to the person and number of the subject. However, in the above sentences, the underlined words remain the same even when the subject changes.

When the verb in the sentence indicates the tense and changes according to the subject, we call it the finite verb. A finite verb has a subject.

The verb in a sentence that has no subject, person or number is called a non-finite verb.

In these sentences, the highlighted verbs are finite verbs that change with the subject, while the underlined verbs are non-finite verbs.

  • I go to the market every day to fetch milk.
  • He goes to the market every day to fetch milk.
    There are three kinds of non-finite verbs—infinitives, participles and gerunds. Let us learn about them in detail.

Infinitives

Read these sentences.

  • I want to buy some perfume.
  • Indira wants to buy some clothes.
    In these sentences, the verb want is the finite verb and to buy is the infinitive.

Intuitives are also called the to-verb because to is usually a part of the infinitive form. Let us learn about some of the functions of infinitives.

  • Infinitives can function as the subject or the object of a sentence.

    • I want to bathe. (object)
    • To delay is bad. (subject)

  • The infinitive can be the object of the verb and also modified by an adverb.

    • Many men prefer to work slowly.

  • An infinitive can also qualify an adjective or a noun.

    • Apples are sweet to eat.
    • This is not the time to sleep.
      NOTE:
      Infinitives are useful when—

  • we wish to state an aim or purpose.

    • He called to apologise.
    • He wanted to buy milk.
    • They agreed to help us.
  • when we wish to indicate result.
    • She lived to see the outcome.
    • The news proved to be true.
  • Infinitives can also be the object of a preposition.
    • The teacher is about to start.

Take a look at these sentences.

  • To steal is a sin.

  • To eat too much is harmful.
    These sentences are grammatically correct, but sound strange. Now, read these sentences.

  • It is a sin to steal.

  • It is harmful to eat too much.
    It is better to use it as the subject and the infinitive as the object in such sentences.

When the to+verb form is used in a sentence and functions as a noun, it is called the infinitive.

We usually use to with the infinitive. However it is not essential. When an infinitive is used without to it is called a bare infinitive.

  • We do not use to when we use infinitives with auxiliary verbs like must, can, should, shall, will, may, might and do. For example,
    • I must go home now.
    • They might leave for Dehradun next week.
  • We do not use to with the infinitive after verbs of perception like see, hear, watch, know and feel. For example,
    • I saw Leena leave the house.
    • I felt an ant crawl up my leg.
  • We do not use to when we use infinitives after verbs like make, let, dare or need. For example,
    • I made him speak.
    • Let me try this.
    • How dare you touch my books?
    • You need not solve these problems.

NOTE:
With verbs like need and dare, note that we use the infinitive with to in affirmative sentences.
Look at these sentences.

  • He dared to dream, and achieved his ambition.
  • I need to visit the doctor soon.

Participles

You have learnt about present participles (verb+-ing) and past participles 'verb+-ed/-d/-t/-en/-n).

    The highlighted words are past participles that have been used as adjectives.

NOTE:
We may say that a participle is a verbal adjective.

A participle is that form of the verb that can act as an adjective in a sentence.

Participles may be used—

  • as attributes. For example,
    • The torn sheet flew away.
    • A burnt child dreads the fire.
  • in the predicate, modifying the subject or the object. For example,
    • The boy looked terrified.
    • He kept me standing.
  • to talk about an earlier action. For example,
    • Seeing the tiger, the man fled.
    • Dejected by his failure, he left his home.

In the above examples, both actions take place at the same time. When we join the sentences, one finite verb is removed and we use its present participle form instead.

But sometimes, the second action begins only after the first has been completed. In that case, we convert the finite verb denoting the first action into the participle.

  • He had lost all his books. He went to his friend for help.
  • Having lost all his books, he went to his friend for help.

Gerunds
Look at these sentences. Notice how the -ing words have been used in these sentences.

    In these sentences, the -ing words function like nouns. However, all these words are derived from verbs.

When the -ing form of the verb is used as a noun in a sentence, we call it the gerund.

NOTE:
A gerund is a verbal noun.

NOTE:
The -ing word can be used in different ways. For example,

  • Dancing is her hobby. (subject)
  • The girl is dancing gracefully. (verb)
  • Everybody gathered to see the dancing peacock. (adjective)

grammar.title: Transitive and Intransitive Verbs
grammar.html:
We know that a sentence will always have a verb. A verb tells us—

  • what a person or thing does—He repairs cars.
  • what a person has—The girl has a pretty frock.
  • what a person or thing is—The ostrich is a huge bird.

Now, look at this sentence.

  • My mother cut the cake.
    In this sentence, the cake receives the action of the verb.

The person or thing that receives the action of the verb is called the object.

When a verb has an object that receives the action of the verb, it is called a transitive verb.

Now, read this sentence.

  • The child wept loudly.
    In this sentence, there is no object. No one receives the action of the verb.

When a verb has no object, it is called an intransitive verb.

Read these sentences.

  • My father gave me a fruit.
  • My father gave a fruit to me.

Answer these questions.

  • Who is the doer of the action? ____ (This is the subject.)
  • What did Father give? ____ (This is the direct object.)
  • To whom did Father give? ____ (This is the indirect object.)

Most transitive verbs take a single object. But some transitive verbs like give, ask, promise, tell, etc. take two objects—a direct object and an indirect object. In the above sentences, the direct object is fruit, while the indirect object is me.

The person or thing that receives the action of the verb is called the direct object.

The person or thing to whom or on whom the action of the verb is done or who receives the direct object is called the indirect object.

NOTE:
Do remember that most verbs can be used both transitively as well as intransitively. For example,

  • The lawyer spoke the truth.
  • The teacher spoke softly.

Sometime the subject and the object refer to the same person or thing. We then say that the verb has been used reflexively.

  • The girl cut herself.

In such sentences, the object is sometimes omitted.

  • The tyre burst (itself).

Verbs of Incomplete Predication
We know that intransitive verbs do not require objects.

Look at these sentences.

  • The child cries.
  • Men eat.
  • Tigers roar.

he highlighted verbs in these sentences do not require any words to make complete sense.

An intransitive verb that makes complete sense on its own is called a verb of complete predication.

Sometimes, an intransitive verb requires another word or words to make complete sense and to complete the predicate.

An intransitive verb that requires a word or phrase to complete its meaning is called a verb of incomplete predication. The word or words required to make the sense complete is called the complement of the verb.

For example,

  • The boy appears sad.
  • She is talented.
  • She seems happy.
  • The child continued laughing.

In the above examples, the complements tell us something about the subject. So, these are called subjective complements.

We know that transitive verbs have objects. Sometimes, just an object is not good enough. Something more is required to complete the predicate.

Look at this sentence.

  • The members elected Sam captain.
    Here the word captain refers to Sam, the object of the verb. So captain is the objective complement.

grammar.title: Active and Passive Voice
grammar.html:
Take a look at these sentences. How are these sentences different?

  • He wrote a letter.
  • A letter was written by him.

In most sentences, the subject of the sentence is the doer of an action and the object of the sentence is the receiver of the action. For example,

  • Cats eat fish. (cat—subject; fish—object)
  • Rohan posted the letter. (Rohan—subject; letter—object)

The verb that expresses that the action is carried out by the subject is said to be in the active voice. The active voice is used when the agent or the doer is to be made prominent.

However, in some sentences, the subject receives the action of the verb. For example,

  • Fish are eaten by cats. (fish—subject; cats—object)
  • The letter was posted by Rohan. (letter—subject; Rohan—object)

The verb that expresses what is done to the subject is said to be in the passive voice.

Voice is that form of the verb which indicates whether the subject is the doer of the action or something is being done to it.

See how the following sentences in the active voice have been changed into the passive voice without changing their meanings.

  • The captain called the players. (active)
    • The players were called by the captain. (passive)
  • He is painting a portrait. (active)
    • A portrait is being painted by him. (passive)

Can you point out the differences in each of the pairs of sentences?

Read these rules to be kept in mind when changing the voice of the verb from active to passive.

  • The positions of the subject and the object of the verb are interchanged. The subject of the verb in the active voice is made the object of the verb in the passive voice.
  • In the passive voice, the preposition by is added before the object.
  • The number of the verb is changed according to the number and person of the subject.

Study the table to understand how the verb is changed into the passive voice form in different tenses.

Tense Active voice Passive voice
Simple present He paints a wall. A wall is painted by him.
Present continuous He is painting a wall. A wall is being painted by him.
Present perfect He has painted a wall. A wall has been painted by him.
Simple past He painted a wall. A wall was painted by him.
Past continuous He was painting a wall. A wall was being painted by him.
Past perfect He had painted a wall. A wall had been painted by him.
Simple future He will paint a wall. A wall will be painted by him.
Future continuous He will be painting a wall. —
Future perfect He will have painted a wall. A wall will have been painted by him.

A. Underline the verbs in these sentences and state whether they are in the active or in the passive voice.

  1. The farmer ploughed his land regularly.
  2. The storm had caused extensive damage.
  3. The ball was gifted by my coach.
  4. He drank the glass of milk.
  5. I dug the pit in the darkness of the night.
  6. The teacher opened the door of the cupboard.
  7. The mission was accomplished.
  8. A moment later, the door was flung open by the prince.
  9. The chocolate cake was baked by my mother.
  10. The hunter continued to step cautiously ahead.
  11. I picked up the heavy box from the table.
  12. Mowgli laughed at the joke.
  13. The girl was chewing the same piece of gum for hours.

  18. The crowd lined the road and cheered the leader.
  19. He lit a candle.
  20. He picked up the ring furtively.
  21. The letter was mailed by Pragya.
  22. The book was bought by my father.
  23. They called off the meeting.
  24. Someone cleaned the window.
  25. English is spoken all over the world.

NOTE:

  • If the active verb has two objects—one direct and the other indirect—either of them becomes the subject of the passive verb, and the other remains as an object of the verb in the passive voice. The object that comes after the passive verb is called the retained object. For example,
    • My father gave me a cycle. (active voice)
    • I was given a cycle by my father. (passive voice)
    • A cycle was given to me by my father. (passive voice)
  • Active verbs followed by a preposition retain the preposition.
    • The students laughed at the clown.
    • The clown was laughed at by the students.

NOTE:
Do, does and did are not used in the passive voice.

Study this table that shows the changes in imperative sentences where the subject is omitted.

Active voice Passive voice
Take it home. Let it be taken home.
Do it right now. Let it be done right now.
Open the door. Let the door be opened.
Do not heat the food. Let not the food be heated.
  • The imperative sentence in the passive voice takes this form—Let + object + be + past participle
  • If the sentence is in the negative, then the structure is—Let not + object + be + past participle

Study this table to understand how verbs in the active voice in interrogative sentences are changed into the passive voice.

Active voice Passive voice
Did Suman invite you? Were you invited by Suman?
Do the children like chocolates? Are chocolates liked by the children?
Have you finished the work? Has the work been finished by you?
Can anybody cure this disease? Can this disease be cured? (Anybody is not used.)
Who hit the ball? By whom was the ball hit?
When will they announce the date? When will the date be announced? (They is not used.)

  8. Santa Claus gave me a gift.

  17. Somebody has stolen my ring.
  18. They are watching us closely.
  19. What does this packet contain?
  20. The gardener tends to the flowers in my garden.

Let us look at the instances when the use of the passive voice is preferred.

We use the passive voice when—

  • the person or thing acted upon is to be made prominent. The passive voice is thus preferred when the active form would involve the use of a vague pronoun or noun such as somebody, they, people, anybody, as the subject. For example,
    • My book has been stolen. (Someone has stolen my book.)
    • I was asked my identity. (They asked me my identity.)
    • I have been invited to the conference. (Someone has invited me to the conference.)
  • the doer is not known or when it is not intended to name the doer. For example,
    • The victim was carried out.
  • we wish to focus on the person or the thing acted upon rather than the doer or the agent. For example,
    • The building was destroyed by lightning.
  • When the subject in the active voice is implied from the context.
    • He was fired from his job (by his employer).
    • The city has been captured (by the enemy).

NOTE:
Since the object of a verb in the active voice becomes the subject of the passive form, it means that only transitive verbs can be used in the passive, because an intransitive verb has no object.

See how sentences in the passive voice can be changed into the active voice.

  • Passive: The work will be finished by the plumber in a week.

  • Active: The plumber will finish the work in a week.

  • Passive: By whom was this major task accomplished?

  • Active: Who accomplished this major task?

  • Passive: I have been asked to attend this meeting.

  • Active: Someone has asked me to attend this meeting.

A strange sense of fear plagued him. Was it a haunted room? The sound of a creaking door nearby startled him. Everyone had warned him not to spend the night there.

writing.title: Notice Writing
writing.html:
📌 What is a Notice?

A notice is a formal, concise piece of writing used by institutions, schools, or organizations to announce events, issue instructions, or make appeals to a targeted audience. It must be brief, factual, and to the point.

📝 Format / Structure (Word Limit: 50 words)

A notice MUST be enclosed in a BOX. 

+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                        NAME OF THE INSTITUTION/SCHOOL                       |
|                                                                             |
|                                  NOTICE                                     |
|                                                                             |
| Date (e.g., 14 May 2026)                                                    |
|                                                                             |
|                             HEADING / TITLE                                 |
|                                                                             |
| Body of the Notice: (Target audience, what the event is, date, time, venue, |
| and whom to contact for further details. Keep it brief and to the point.)   |
|                                                                             |
| Signature                                                                   |
| Name                                                                        |
| Designation                                                                 |
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------+

⚖️ CBSE Marking Scheme (Typically 3 Marks)

  • Format: 1 Mark (Box, Name of Institution, "NOTICE", Date, Heading, Name/Designation)
  • Content: 1 Marks (What, When, Where, Whom to contact)
  • Expression: 1 Mark (Grammar, Spelling, Formal Tone)

💡 Language Tips & Key Rules

  • Tone: Formal and objective. Avoid first-person pronouns (I, we) unless used in the designation (e.g., "The undersigned").
  • Passive Voice: Prefer passive structures (e.g., It is hereby notified that... or Students are informed that...).
  • The 5 Ws: Ensure your notice answers: What is the event? Where is the venue? When is the date and time? Who is eligible? Whom to contact?
  • Word Limit: Strictly adhere to the 50-word limit for the body.

⚠️ Common Mistakes to Avoid

  • Forgetting the Box: This is a guaranteed deduction of marks.
  • Informal language: Do not use conversational greetings like "Hello friends".
  • Missing deadlines: If an event requires registration, always mention a "last date to register".

🌟 Model Example

Q: You are the Cultural Secretary of Bal Bharati Public School, Delhi. Your school is organizing an Inter-House Dramatics Competition. Write a notice in about 50 words inviting names from students of Classes IX and X. 

+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                        BAL BHARATI PUBLIC SCHOOL, DELHI                     |
|                                                                             |
|                                    NOTICE                                   |
|                                                                             |
| 20 August 2026                                                              |
|                                                                             |
|                       INTER-HOUSE DRAMATICS COMPETITION                     |
|                                                                             |
| This is to inform all students of Classes IX and X that the school is       |
| organizing an Inter-House Dramatics Competition on 5 September 2026 in the  |
| school auditorium from 10:00 AM onwards. The theme for the play is "Unity   |
| in Diversity". Interested students must register their names with their     |
| respective House Captains latest by 28 August 2026.                         |
|                                                                             |
| (Signature)                                                                 |
| Kavita Sharma                                                               |
| Cultural Secretary                                                          |
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------+

✍️ Practice Prompts

  1. Tour/Camp: You are the Sports Captain. Write a notice informing students of Class IX about a 3-day Trekking Camp to Shimla. Mention dates, fees, and the last date for submitting consent forms.
  2. Found: You found a silver wristwatch in the school computer lab. Write a notice for the school notice board asking the rightful owner to claim it by providing necessary identification details.

writing.title: Diary Writing
writing.html:
Read this extract from the 1864 science-fiction novel by Jules Verne (1828-1905) called the Journey to the Interior of the Earth (also called Journey to the Centre of the Earth).

Monday, August 17: I am trying to recall the peculiar instincts of the monsters of the pre-adamite world, who, coming next in succession after the molluscs, the crustaceans and the fishes, preceded the animals of mammalian race upon the earth. The world then belonged to reptiles. Those monsters held the mastery in the seas of the secondary period. They possessed a perfect organisation, gigantic proportions, prodigious strength. The saurians of our day, the alligators and the crocodiles, are but feeble reproductions of their forefathers of primitive ages.
I shudder as I recall these monsters to my remembrance. No human eye has ever beheld them living. I saw at the Hamburg museum the skeleton of one of these creatures thirty feet in length. Am I then fated—I, a denizen of earth—to be placed face to face with these representatives of long extinct families? No; surely it cannot be! Yet the deep marks of conical teeth upon the iron pick are certainly those of the crocodile.
My eyes are fearfully bent upon the sea. I dread to see one of these monsters darting forth from its submarine caverns. I suppose Professor Liedenbrock was of my opinion too, and even shared my fears, for after having examined the pick, his eyes traversed the ocean from side to side. What a very bad notion that was of his, I thought to myself, to take soundings just here! He has disturbed some monstrous beast in its remote den, and if we are not attacked on our voyage.
I look at our guns and see that they are all right. My uncle notices it, and looks on approvingly.
Already widely disturbed regions on the surface of the water indicate some commotion below. The danger is approaching. We must be on the lookout.

What you have just read is a very different form of writing which is written in the first person.
This form of writing is called diary writing. This is yet another form of creative writing and it does have some special features. Let us list them.

  • It is written in the first person and the day and date are carefully recorded.
  • It is not only a chronicle of the events that have taken place on that day and date, but also a spontaneous expression of emotions.
  • Sometimes the diary is given a name. Anne Frank called her diary, 'Kitty'.
  • Usually, a diary is maintained by an individual and is not meant for public viewing. So, one can really be honest to the diary and write without inhibitions. However, in a classroom situation, perhaps one has to be diplomatic.
  • When writing in a diary, you should keep in mind the normal rules of good writing. Be careful about sentence constructions, paragraphs, ornamentations in language, etc.

NOTE:
Mind the format! Every entry must begin with the date and day of the week. Diary entries may also be signed off like letters. You have a wide choice of tenses to use. You may start with the past as you are trying to recall the incidents of the day and end with the present or the past when you are trying to sum up your emotions.

Now, attempt writing diary entries for the following situations.

  1. Suppose your parents have left town and you are alone at home for a week. Write a diary entry for each day of the week describing what you did and how you managed.
  2. Imagine your plane has crashed in the Amazonian rainforest. You are the lone survivor. In the form of a diary, narrate how you spent your days (at least seven) in the wilderness before you were rescued.
  3. Imagine you have been selected to represent the school at some event (it could be a sports meet, a debate or a quiz). Write three diary entries—the first describing how you prepared for the selection process, the second describing how you felt after you were selected and the third describing what happened when you participated in the competition.

Answers – Diary Writing

1.

Monday, 10 October 20XX
9:30 p.m.

Dear Diary,
My parents left for Mumbai early this morning to attend an official seminar, leaving me in charge of the house for an entire week. At first, I felt a surge of excitement thinking about the freedom of having the house to myself. However, as evening approached, the silence in the living room felt quite unusual. I cooked simple noodles for dinner and made sure all the doors were locked securely. It is going to be a true test of my independence, but I am determined to manage everything responsibly!

Tuesday, 11 October 20XX
10:00 p.m.

Dear Diary,
Today was my second day on my own, and it went fairly smoothly. I woke up early on my own alarm, made myself breakfast, and packed my school bag without any reminders. After returning from school, I watered the garden plants and completed my homework before heating up the meal mom had stored in the refrigerator. Managing daily chores alongside studies is definitely harder than it looks, but I am learning to organize my time efficiently.

Wednesday, 12 October 20XX
9:45 p.m.

Dear Diary,
A minor challenge arose this evening when the kitchen tap started leaking after dinner! For a moment, I panicked seeing water pool on the sink counter. Remembering dad's advice, I located the main valve under the sink and turned it off safely. I then called our neighborhood plumber to fix it. Resolving the issue independently gave me a huge boost of confidence. I spoke to mom on the phone later and she was very proud of how I handled it.

Thursday, 13 October 20XX
10:15 p.m.

Dear Diary,
Today was a busy school day, but keeping the house tidy has become second nature now. I swept the rooms in the afternoon and kept my study table neatly organized. To avoid feeling lonely in the evening, I played my acoustic guitar for an hour and read a chapter of my adventure novel. Being alone has given me time for quiet self-reflection, and I am enjoying this newly discovered self-reliance.

Friday, 14 October 20XX
9:15 p.m.

Dear Diary,
With the weekend approaching, I decided to finish all my pending homework tonight so that I could relax tomorrow. I prepared a simple vegetable stir-fry for dinner, which surprisingly turned out quite delicious! My aunt called in the evening to check on me and invited me over for lunch tomorrow, but I politely declined because I want to complete this week entirely on my own strength.

Saturday, 15 October 20XX
10:30 p.m.

Dear Diary,
What a productive Saturday! I spent the morning doing laundry and cleaning out the refrigerator to make sure everything was fresh. In the afternoon, my friend Rohan visited for a couple of hours, and we played board games in the living room. Handling all household responsibilities while keeping the house spotless has given me a great sense of accomplishment.

Sunday, 16 October 20XX
9:00 p.m.

Dear Diary,
My parents finally returned home this evening! They were pleasantly surprised to find the house neat, clean, and well-managed. Mom gave me a warm hug and praised my maturity, while dad gave me an approving pat on the back. This week has been an incredible learning experience. I proved to myself that I can be responsible, self-sufficient, and dependable in any situation.

2.

Monday, 4 June 20XX
8:00 p.m.

Dear Diary,
I am writing this with trembling hands by the dim light of a small campfire. Our light aircraft suffered engine failure during a sudden storm and crashed deep inside the Amazon rainforest. Miraculously, I survived with only minor scrapes, but the plane is destroyed and there is no trace of the pilots. I managed to salvage a pocket knife, a flashlight, and a small water bottle from the wreckage. Fear surrounds me in this dense, dark jungle, but I must stay strong to survive.

Tuesday, 5 June 20XX
7:30 p.m.

Dear Diary,
My second day in the wilderness was spent securing basic necessities. I built a temporary shelter using fallen palm fronds and branches near the crash site so that rescue teams can spot me easily from the air. Drinking water was my biggest concern, but I managed to collect fresh rainwater using large leaves. The endless calls of unseen birds and insects echo through the trees, keeping me awake, but I am holding onto hope.

Wednesday, 6 June 20XX
8:15 p.m.

Dear Diary,
Hunger set in severely today. Remembering survival documentaries, I carefully avoided bright berries and instead searched for wild bananas and edible palm shoots near a nearby stream. Navigating the thick foliage was exhausting, and I had to be constantly vigilant against snakes and insects. I maintained a smoky fire near my shelter throughout the day, hoping the smoke signal would attract searching aircraft.

Thursday, 7 June 20XX
7:45 p.m.

Dear Diary,
A heavy tropical downpour battered the rainforest for hours today, dampening my shelter and putting out my fire. It was a miserable, shivering day, but I managed to protect my notebook and matches inside a waterproof pouch from my backpack. Rebuilding the fire after the rain stopped was tough, but seeing the flames flicker back to life restored my spirits. I will not give up.

Friday, 8 June 20XX
8:30 p.m.

Dear Diary,
Today I heard the distant rumble of a helicopter engine in the afternoon! I rushed to add damp leaves to my fire to create thick white smoke, but the aircraft moved away before spotting me. Though disappointed, hearing search teams gave me immense comfort—it means people are actively looking for me! I constructed a giant 'SOS' sign on a clear patch of ground using light-colored rocks and tree trunks.

Saturday, 9 June 20XX
8:00 p.m.

Dear Diary,
Physical fatigue is taking a heavy toll on my body, but my mind remains resolute. I spent the day reinforcing my shelter and gathering firewood to keep the wild animals at bay during the night. Looking up at the tiny patches of night sky visible through the thick jungle canopy, I prayed dearly for my family. I know rescue is near; I just have to endure a little longer.

Sunday, 10 June 20XX
6:00 p.m.

Dear Diary,
I am writing this from inside a rescue helicopter! Late this afternoon, a search and rescue team spotted my 'SOS' sign and smoke signal while patrolling the sector. A rescue swimmer descended via cable, lifted me to safety, and wrapped me in warm blankets. As the helicopter rose above the green canopy of the Amazon, tears of overwhelming gratitude filled my eyes. I survived seven long days in the wild, and I am finally going home!

3.

Friday, 5 August 20XX
9:00 p.m.

Tomorrow is the final selection trial to choose our school's representative for the State Inter-School Debate Championship. I have put weeks of hard work into this preparation, and I truly hope I can deliver my best performance.

8:30 p.m.

Carrying the responsibility of representing my institution is both thrilling and humbling. I am determined to work even harder now to bring home the trophy!

Wednesday, 17 August 20XX
9:30 p.m.

What an unforgettable day! The State Championship took place today at the city auditorium, featuring brilliant speakers from over thirty schools.
