The rebuttal round was intense, but I countered the opposing arguments effectively. To my immense delight, our school won the First Runner-Up trophy! Holding the glittering trophy on stage alongside my mentor teacher was a moment of supreme pride that I will cherish forever.

writing.title: Narrative Writing
writing.html:
There are different ways of going about writing a story, and there are no set guidelines that can be followed to ensure a good short story. However, one of the first things to remember is that for your story to be a success, you have to hold the reader's attention.

Here are some points to keep in mind when writing a short story.

  • Decide on a situation—this could be a problem that has to be resolved by the main character or a set of characters. This situation can depend on the title or theme that you are given. The plot is the most important aspect of a short story. Decide the main events and try to think of a twist at the end. Your story must have a beginning, a middle and a satisfactory ending. Everything could end unhappily for all the characters, but at least the reader must know what happened to the people in the story.
  • Choose a narrative point of view. You can write your story in the first person (as if you were one of the characters), or in the third person (as a detached narrator who presents the thoughts and observations of several characters). If you write in the first person, be consistent about the use of the pronoun 'I'.
  • Create a list of characters. Try to give them individual characteristics. Focus more on the main character.
  • Establish believable characters and settings, with vivid descriptions and dialogues, to create a story that your readers will care about. Remember that you have to work within a limited number of words; you cannot go on for pages, so you must use language effectively. Appeal to your readers' five senses to make your settings more real.
  • Never underestimate the power of dialogue in revealing the character of a person or the complexity of a situation, but in a short story, there is no place for long speeches. Every word you put into the mouth of your characters must contribute to revealing your theme.

A. Write original short stories based on the given instructions.

  1. Begin with—'It was a stormy night. The rain was pouring down heavily and the wind was so strong that many trees were uprooted. I was returning home after visiting Vivek when...'
  2. End with—'I shall always cherish that memory.'
  3. Begin with—'The water was cold, I took a deep breath and jumped...'
  4. End with—'...where there is a will, there is always a way.'

B. Write original short stories using these guidelines.

  1. in which a briefcase, a camera and a policeman play a significant part
  2. in which one of the following plays a significant part—
    • a birthday
    • a family argument
    • a power cut
  3. You are being followed; you manage to get away or were caught by your pursuers.
  4. 'When the door of happiness closes, another opens; but often we look so long at the closed door that we do not see the one which has opened for us.'—Helen Keller. Write a short story using the above quotation as its theme.
  5. to bring out clearly the meaning of this proverb—'Honesty is the best policy.'

Answers – Narrative Writing

A.

  1. It was a stormy night. The rain was pouring down heavily and the wind was so strong that many trees were uprooted. I was returning home after visiting Vivek when my bicycle chain suddenly snapped near the desolate stretch beside the old city lake. Darkness engulfed the road as streetlights flickered and died due to power failure.

Standing under a leaking bus shelter, I heard a faint whimpering sound coming from a muddy ditch. Shining my phone flashlight, I discovered a tiny puppy trapped beneath a fallen tree branch, shivering in the freezing rain. Without hesitation, I waded through the mud, lifted the heavy branch with all my strength, and wrapped the frightened puppy in my raincoat. Carrying the little creature safely in my arms, I walked the remaining two miles home. The puppy survived and became my loyal companion, reminding me that even the stormiest nights can bring unexpected blessings.

  1. The sun was setting behind the snow-capped Himalayan peaks, painting the sky in brilliant shades of crimson and gold. We had spent five arduous hours trekking through dense pine forests to reach the scenic high-altitude meadow of Dayara Bugyal. Our legs were exhausted, but the panoramic beauty unfolding before our eyes erased every bit of fatigue.

Our trekking guide pitched our tents beside a crystal-clear mountain stream, while we gathered around a small campfire to share hot tea and stories. As night descended, millions of bright stars glittered across the clear night sky, creating a breathtaking canopy above us. Sitting quietly under that vast cosmic expanse, surrounded by trusted friends and peaceful silence, I felt a deep sense of serenity and gratitude. I shall always cherish that memory.

  1. The water was cold, I took a deep breath and jumped into the rushing river. The sudden shock of icy mountain water surged through my body, sending a sharp shiver down my spine. But there was no time to panic; my young cousin had accidentally lost his footing on the slippery riverbank and was being carried downstream by the swift current.

Kicking hard against the powerful swirl of the current, I swam vigorously toward the bright yellow jacket floating near the bend. Reaching him just before the river tumbled into a rocky rapid, I grabbed his collar securely with one arm and pulled his head above water. Using my remaining energy, I kicked toward a calm eddy along the left bank, where helpful bystanders pulled us both onto solid ground. Gasping for air on the grassy bank, I held my coughing cousin tightly, relieved that my decisive leap had saved his life.

  1. When Rohan lost his right arm in a tragic train accident at the age of twelve, everyone believed his passion for painting was permanently destroyed. His canvas easel sat abandoned in his room, covered in dust, while he struggled with deep sadness for months. However, watching a documentary about adaptive artists reignited a spark of determination within his heart.

He began practicing patiently every single day, training his left hand to hold brushes, mix oil paints, and execute delicate strokes. Initial attempts resulted in smudges and frustrating failures, but Rohan refused to give up. After three years of relentless practice, he submitted his artwork to the National Youth Art Exhibition. To everyone's astonishment, his painting won the first prize for extraordinary technique and emotional depth. Standing proudly on stage to receive his trophy, Rohan proved to the world that where there is a will, there is always a way.

B.

  1. The Missing Briefcase
    Inspector Sharma was standing near the central fountain of the crowded botanical garden when a frantic tourist approached him. The tourist explained that while taking photographs with his vintage camera, he had placed a black leather briefcase containing important property documents on a nearby bench. When he turned back moments later, the briefcase had vanished.

Inspector Sharma asked the photographer to show him the pictures he had taken over the last ten minutes. Carefully reviewing the high-resolution images on the camera screen, the policeman noticed a man in a red jacket picking up the briefcase in the background of a floral landscape photo. Inspector Sharma quickly alerted the park exit gates with the visual description. Within fifteen minutes, security guards intercepted the suspect attempting to board a taxi. The briefcase was recovered intact, proving that the camera and the quick-thinking policeman were instrumental in solving the crime.

  1. Light in the Darkness
    The Roy family was preparing for dinner on a hot summer evening when an unexpected power cut plunged the entire apartment complex into total darkness. Sweltering heat quickly filled the rooms, making everyone irritable. Rohan and his elder sister began complaining bitterly, interrupting their mother's attempts to light emergency candles.

Seeing the mood souring, their grandfather smiled and suggested a traditional story session on the open balcony. As gentle night breezes blew, he recounted fascinating tales from his youth, filled with humor, adventure, and wisdom. The children listened spellbound, forgetting their discomfort and putting aside their electronic gadgets. When the electricity was finally restored two hours later, no one wanted the magical evening to end. The sudden power cut had unexpectedly brought the family closer together.

  1. Escaping the Shadow
    Walking back home through the quiet alleyways of Old Town at dusk, Sameer noticed a tall figure in a dark trench coat keeping pace behind him. Every time Sameer accelerated his steps, the footsteps behind him quickened as well. Panic seized his mind as he realized he was being pursued through the dimly lit streets.

Knowing the geography of his neighborhood well, Sameer pretended to walk toward a dead-end alley. Just as his pursuer turned the corner behind him, Sameer ducked swiftly behind a heavy wooden gate and slipped into the back courtyard of a busy bakery. Slipping out through the bakery's bright front entrance onto the main crowded boulevard, he flagged down a passing police patrol car and reported the suspicious tracker. Safe among the crowd, Sameer took a deep sigh of relief, thankful for his quick wits.

  1. Opening New Doors
    When Priya failed to clear the final interview for her dream medical college admission, she felt utterly heartbroken. For weeks she stayed indoors, mourning the closed door of her ambition and ignoring all words of comfort from family and friends. She could not stop brooding over what she had lost.

Encouraged by her high school biology teacher, Priya reluctantly enrolled in a degree program in Environmental Biotechnology. To her surprise, she discovered a deep passion for bio-remediation research and sustainable ecology. Within two years, she led an innovative research project that developed low-cost water purification filters for rural villages, earning an international scholarship. Looking back, Priya smiled, realizing how true Helen Keller's words were: when the door of her medical career closed, a far more fulfilling door of scientific discovery had opened for her.

  1. Honesty is the Best Policy
    Raghav, a poor college student working part-time as a delivery boy, found a heavy leather wallet dropped near a park bench late one evening. Opening it to check for identification, he was stunned to find fifty thousand rupees in cash along with credit cards and an ID card belonging to a prominent businessman, Mr. Singhania.

Though Raghav desperately needed money to pay his upcoming semester fees, his conscience refused to let him keep what was not his. He immediately rode his bicycle to Mr. Singhania's residence and handed over the wallet intact. Deeply moved by Raghav's integrity, Mr. Singhania offered to sponsor his complete higher education and hired him as a management intern in his company. Raghav's truthfulness changed his life forever, proving that honesty is indeed the best policy.

writing.title: Formal Email Writing
writing.html:
📌 What is a Formal Email?

A formal email is the electronic equivalent of a formal letter. It is used for official communication with school principals, teachers, business managers, or authorities. Because emails are read quickly, the language must be extremely concise, clear, and professional.

📝 Format / Structure (Word Limit: 100-120 words)

The format is enclosed in a BOX to simulate a computer screen/email client: 

+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| Date    : 24 May 2026                                                       |
| From    : student.name@email.com                                            |
| To      : principal.school@email.com                                        |
| Cc      : principal.school@email.com                                        |
| Bcc     : principal.school@email.com                                        |
| Subject : Request for extension of project submission deadline.             |
|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Respected Sir/Madam,                                                        |
|                                                                             |
| Paragraph 1: State the purpose of the email directly.                       |
| Paragraph 2: Provide brief, necessary details or reasons.                   |
| Paragraph 3: State the action required and conclude politely.               |
|                                                                             |
| Regards,                                                                    |
| Name                                                                        |
| Designation/Class                                                           |
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------+

(Note: Some formats also include 'Cc' (Carbon Copy) and 'Bcc' (Blind Carbon Copy) below the 'To' field. Include them if your teacher specifically asks, but Date, From, To, and Subject are the essential headers.)

⚖️ CBSE Marking Scheme (Typically 5 Marks)

  • Format: 1 Mark (Box, headers, salutation, sign-off)
  • Content: 2 Marks (Clarity of purpose, relevant details)
  • Expression: 2 Marks (Polite tone, grammar, brevity)

💡 Language Tips & Key Rules

  • Subject Line: This is the most important part of an email. It must be a short phrase summarizing the email (e.g., Application for sick leave). Do not write a full sentence in the subject line.
  • Brevity: Do not write long, winding stories. Get straight to the point in the first sentence.
  • Tone: Formal and polite. Never use text slang (like 'u', 'pls', 'thx').

⚠️ Common Mistakes to Avoid

  • Leaving the subject line blank or writing "Hi" as the subject.
  • Forgetting to draw the box around the email.
  • Using informal sign-offs like "Lots of love" or "Yours lovingly". Always use "Regards," or "Sincerely,".

🌟 Model Example

Q: You are Amit/Amita, the Secretary of the IT Club of your school. Write an email to the Principal of a neighboring school inviting their students to participate in an Inter-School Coding Competition organized by your club. 

+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| Date    : 10 October 2026                                                   |
| From    : itclub.dps@email.com                                              |
| To      : principal.modernschool@email.com                                  |
| Cc      : principal.school@email.com                                        |
| Bcc     : principal.school@email.com                                        |
| Subject : Invitation for Inter-School Coding Competition 2026               |
|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Respected Sir/Madam,                                                        |
|                                                                             |
| I am writing on behalf of the IT Club of Delhi Public School to formally    |
| invite your students to participate in our annual Inter-School Coding       |
| Competition, 'Code-Fest 2026'.                                              |
|                                                                             |
| The event is scheduled to be held on 25th October 2026 in our school        |
| computer labs from 9:00 AM to 2:00 PM. The competition is open to students  |
| of Classes IX and X. We believe this platform will provide a great          |
| opportunity for young tech enthusiasts to showcase their programming skills.|
|                                                                             |
| We have attached the detailed brochure and registration forms with this     |
| email. We kindly request you to forward this to your Computer Science       |
| department. The last date for registration is 18th October.                 |
|                                                                             |
| We look forward to enthusiastic participation from your esteemed school.    |
|                                                                             |
| Regards,                                                                    |
| Amit Sharma                                                                 |
| Secretary, IT Club, DPS                                                     |
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------+

✍️ Practice Prompts

  1. Write a formal email to the Manager of an electronics store inquiring about the bulk pricing of 20 tablets for your school's digital library.
  2. Write an email to your class teacher submitting your Science project online and apologizing for a one-day delay due to internet issues at home.

writing.title: Informal Letter
writing.html:
📌 What is an Informal Letter?

An informal letter is a personal letter written to friends, family members, or relatives to share personal news, express feelings, ask for advice, or describe an experience. At the Class IX level, the letter should display emotional depth, mature vocabulary, and well-structured paragraphs despite the casual tone.

📝 Format / Structure (Word Limit: 120-150 words)

The format follows a left-aligned layout:

  1. Sender’s Address: Top left corner.
  2. Date: Below the address (e.g., 24 May 2026).
  3. Salutation: E.g., Dear Rahul, Dear Mom,
  4. Body of the Letter:
    - Paragraph 1 (Introduction): Inquire about their health and state the reason for writing the letter.
    - Paragraph 2 (Main Content): Expand on the topic. Give vivid details of the experience, problem, or news you are sharing. Show your feelings.
    - Paragraph 3 (Conclusion): Concluding remarks, hopes for a reply, and sending love to other family members.
  5. Subscription: Yours lovingly, / Yours affectionately,
  6. Name: First name only.

⚖️ CBSE Marking Scheme (Typically 5-8 Marks)

  • Format: 1-2 Marks (Address, Date, Salutation, Closing)
  • Content: 3-4 Marks (Relevance, ideas, elaboration)
  • Expression: 2 Marks (Grammar, vocabulary, friendly but mature tone)

💡 Language Tips & Key Phrases

  • Opening:
  • "I was delighted to read your last letter..."
  • "I hope this letter finds you in the pink of health."
  • Tone: Conversational and warm. You can use contractions (I've, couldn't, haven't).
  • Elaboration: Don't just state facts. If you went on a trip, describe how it made you feel.

⚠️ Common Mistakes to Avoid

  • Using formal sign-offs: Never use "Yours faithfully" or "Yours sincerely" in an informal letter.
  • Missing the Date: Ensure the date is written in the correct format (15 May 2026, not 15/05/26).

🌟 Model Example

Q: You are Sneha/Sumit studying in a boarding school in Dehradun. Write a letter to your mother telling her about your experience of participating in a grueling 3-day adventure camp organized by the school.

Room No. 42, Ganga Hostel
Doon Public School
Dehradun

12 October 2026

Dear Mom,

I hope you and dad are doing wonderful back home. I am writing this letter to share my thrilling experience at the 3-day adventure camp our school organized in Rishikesh last weekend.

Honestly, mom, when I first saw the itinerary, I was terrified. The camp included rock climbing, valley crossing, and white-water rafting. On the first day during the rock climbing session, my hands were shaking, and I almost gave up halfway. However, our instructor and my friends cheered me on, and when I finally reached the top, the feeling of accomplishment was indescribable! The river rafting the next day was the highlight—the freezing water splashing against our faces was both scary and exhilarating.

This trip pushed me out of my comfort zone and taught me that I am much stronger than I thought. I can't wait to show you all the photographs during the winter break.

Give my love to dad and little Rohan. Miss you all!

Yours lovingly,
Sneha

✍️ Practice Prompts

  1. Write a letter to your friend apologizing for your rude behavior during an argument last week, and asking for their forgiveness.
  2. You recently read a highly inspiring book. Write a letter to your cousin recommending the book to them and explaining why you liked it so much.

writing.title: Informal Invitation Letter
writing.html:
📌 What is an Informal Invitation Letter?

An informal invitation letter is written to invite friends, relatives, or close acquaintances to personal events such as a birthday party, an anniversary, a housewarming, or a casual get-together. The tone is warm, personal, and friendly, completely avoiding official jargon.

📝 Format / Structure (Word Limit: 50-100 words)

The format is similar to a regular informal letter but is usually shorter and more direct.

  1. Sender’s Address: Top left corner.
  2. Date: Below the address (e.g., 24 May 2026).
  3. Salutation: Dear [First Name],
  4. Body of the Letter:
    - The Invite: Clearly state what the occasion is and explicitly invite the person.
    - The Details: Mention the Date, Time, and Venue of the event clearly.
    - Personal Touch: Add a line about how much their presence would mean to you or what fun activities are planned.
  5. Subscription (Closing): Yours lovingly, / Yours affectionately,
  6. Sender’s Name: First name only.

⚖️ CBSE Marking Scheme (Typically 3-4 Marks)

  • Format: 1 Mark
  • Content (Occasion, Date, Time, Venue): 1-2 Marks
  • Expression (Friendly tone, grammar): 1 Mark

💡 Language Tips & Useful Phrases

  • Opening phrases:
  • "I am thrilled to invite you to..."
  • "You will be glad to know that..."
  • "It gives me immense pleasure to invite you and your family to..."
  • Adding warmth:
  • "The party won't be the same without you."
  • "Looking forward to celebrating together."

⚠️ Common Mistakes to Avoid

  • Forgetting Event Details: An invitation is useless if you forget to mention when and where it is happening.
  • Using formal language: Do not use "Respected" or "Yours faithfully."
  • Writing too much: Unlike a regular informal letter where you discuss life and health at length, an invitation should get straight to the point.

🌟 Model Example

Q: You are Ankit/Ankita. You are organizing a surprise 50th birthday party for your father. Write an informal letter inviting your uncle, who lives in Chandigarh, to the party.

14, Green Park
New Delhi

15 October 2026

Dear Uncle Suresh,

I hope you and Aunt are doing well. You will be glad to know that dad is turning 50 next week. To celebrate this milestone, mom and I are organizing a surprise birthday party for him.

It gives me immense pleasure to invite you and Aunt to the celebration. The party will be held at our residence on Sunday, 25th October 2026, starting at 7:00 PM. We have arranged for dad's favorite live music band and a wonderful dinner.

Since it is a surprise, please do not mention it to dad when you speak to him! The celebration will be incomplete without your presence. We are eagerly waiting to see you.

Yours lovingly,
Ankit

✍️ Practice Prompts

  1. Write an informal letter to your best friend inviting them to your house for a weekend pajama party to celebrate the end of your final exams. Mention the date and activities planned.
  2. Your family has just moved into a new apartment. Write an informal letter to your cousin inviting them to the housewarming ceremony.

writing.title: Essay Writing
writing.html:
An essay, or a composition, can be an expression of your opinions, feelings, or experiences. It is not, however, a rambling piece of writing, but a very structured form. An essay is usually divided into paragraphs. The first paragraph is called the introduction and the final paragraph is called the conclusion. The paragraphs in between the introduction and the conclusion constitute the body of the composition. These paragraphs help to develop the thoughts and ideas of the composition.

What are the qualities of a good composition?

  • Unity of thought: The composition must develop one theme with a definite purpose.
  • Order: The composition must follow a certain ordered line of thought and come to a definite conclusion. It must not consist of haphazard reflections put down anyhow. Therefore it is of utmost importance to plan out a line of thought before beginning to write.
  • Brevity: A composition should not be very long. What is important is whether the composition is well written or not. Though there can be no strict rule regarding the length of a composition, one can say that it ought to be roughly around three hundred words.
  • Style: A composition should be written in simple and correct English. The sentence construction should be simple, direct and natural. The secret of clear writing is clear thinking. Slang, colloquial terms and free and easy constructions ought to be avoided. A composition which ‘moves’ the reader is supposed to be a good piece of writing. The words chosen ought to be justified and necessary.
  • Personal touch: A composition must reveal the personal feelings and opinions of the writer. Without the personal touch, the composition becomes devoid of individuality.

How do we write a good composition?

  • Step 1: Think about the topic. What does it mean?
  • Step 2: Write down the thoughts and questions that arise in your mind after seeing the topic.
  • Step 3: Arrange the thoughts and questions in a logical sequence, so that one may lead to the other.
  • Step 4: Once the facts have been organised one can concentrate on the style. How do we make the facts appear attractive? This can be done in several ways.
  • Start the composition with the help of a creative and arresting introduction by using one of the various methods:
    • by setting the scene of the story
    • by plunging straight into action
    • by an arresting or unusual detail
    • by a dialogue
  • The style of writing also includes a meaningful conclusion. Remember—
    • you should round off your narration
    • you could aim for a surprise ending
    • you must avoid ending your composition with sentences such as, 'In conclusion...', 'It can be seen that...' or 'Summing up, I'd like to state...'
  • Step 5: Keep in mind the length of the composition. An ideal composition would be about five paragraphs of 60 words each. A little more or less does not make much of a difference. Remember, it is not how much you say but what you say and how you say it—that is what creates an impact!
  • Step 6: Do not forget the personal touch. Remember what you are writing is a composition and not an impersonal report. Therefore your opinion and views are most important.

NOTE:
At this point, one has to understand the difference between a descriptive composition and a narrative composition. Certain topics like 'A Village Fair' may seem a little confusing. The confusion arises in whether the composition ought to be written in the first person or in the third person. 'A Village Fair' may be written in the first person. However, the description of the fair is more important than the narrator's experience of it, which may come in as part of the conclusion! If the topic reads, 'How You Spent a Day in a Village Fair', then the narrator's experience becomes as important as the description of the fair. Remember that descriptions are a part of a narrative essay and descriptive essays may or may not be written in the first person.

Write a composition (300–350 words) on these topics with the help of the given guidelines.

  1. Pandemonium at the Picnic
    (A picnic or an excursion is an enjoyable experience if shared, especially if something exciting takes place. Describe such an occasion.)

  2. Going to the Market
    (Write a description of a market scene in your area.)

  3. An Old Favourite
    (Write about a book or a television programme that you have enjoyed and try to analyse what particular features gave you pleasure.)

  4. A Wedding in the Family
    (You have recently attended your cousin's marriage. Describe the event, the customs and what you liked/disliked about it.)

  5. My Favourite Extra-curricular Activities
    (What do you enjoy doing in your spare time? How do you feel these activities contribute to the development of your character?)

Answers – Essay Writing

1. Pandemonium at the Picnic

The winter morning was bright and crisp when our class set out for an annual picnic to a scenic lakeside resort located near the foothills. Everyone was in high spirits, singing songs on the bus ride and anticipating a peaceful day of outdoor games, delicious food, and relaxed conversation under the shaded canopy of pine trees.

Upon arrival, we quickly set up our picnic mats, spread out our lunch boxes, and began an energetic game of badminton. However, our tranquil morning was suddenly interrupted by an unexpected visitor. A troupe of curious wild monkeys descended from the surrounding trees, attracted by the aroma of freshly cooked snacks. Within seconds, utter pandemonium broke out across the picnic grounds.

One daring monkey snatched a container of samosas right off our table, while another grabbed our teacher's brightly colored handbag and scurried up a tall banyan tree. Students scattered in all directions, screaming in excitement and surprise, while our frantic class monitor attempted to rescue the remaining lunch baskets by covering them with picnic mats.

Realizing that panic would only agitate the creatures, our teacher calmly suggested that we leave a tray of fruits at the base of a nearby tree. The clever tactic worked like magic; the monkeys descended to feast on the apples and bananas, dropping the stolen handbag safely onto the soft grass below. We watched from a safe distance, chuckling at the comical turn of events.

Once the uninvited guests returned to the forest, we gathered together to tidy up the area and share whatever food remained. What began as a routine day in nature turned into an unforgettable adventure filled with laughter and excitement. Looking back, that chaotic picnic remains one of my fondest school memories, proving that unexpected surprises often make for the best stories.

2. Going to the Market

The central market in our city is a vibrant, bustling hub of activity that truly comes alive during the late afternoon hours. As one approaches the main entrance, a symphony of sounds greets the senses—hawkers shouting out enticing prices, honking rickshaws navigating narrow lanes, and the steady hum of bargaining shoppers filling the air.

Brightly lit shops and canvas stalls line both sides of the crowded street, displaying a stunning variety of goods. Vegetable vendors arrange fresh, green produce in neat pyramids, sprinkling water over leafy spinach and crisp cucumbers to keep them looking fresh. Adjacent to them, fruit sellers showcase rows of golden mangoes, red apples, and sweet oranges, enticing passersby with their rich fragrance.

Further down the lane, the market turns into a burst of color with textile merchants displaying traditional fabrics, sparkling bangles, and stylish garments. Shoppers move slowly from one stall to another, carefully inspecting goods and negotiating prices with seasoned shopkeepers. The atmosphere is energetic and lively, reflecting the rich cultural diversity of our local community.

The food section of the market is particularly captivating, sending irresistible aromas of freshly fried jalebis, spicy chaat, and roasted nuts through the cool air. Families and groups of friends gather around street food carts, enjoying warm delicacies and sharing lighthearted conversations amidst the ongoing bustle of the market.

Visiting the local market is far more than just a routine shopping trip; it is a sensory experience that captures the beating heart of our city. The dynamic energy, vibrant colors, and friendly human interactions make it a place I love to visit time and again.

3. An Old Favourite

Among the many books I have read over the years, The Adventures of Tom Sawyer by Mark Twain remains my absolute favourite. I first discovered this classic novel during a summer vacation, and its charm has stayed with me ever since. The story revolves around young Tom Sawyer, an imaginative and mischievous boy growing up along the banks of the Mississippi River in the nineteenth century.

What gives me immense pleasure while reading this book is Twain's brilliant depiction of childhood innocence and adventure. Tom's clever antics—such as tricking his friends into whitewashing a fence for him by convincing them it was a privilege—are written with marvelous humor and wit. The author captures the spirit of youth so accurately that every reader can relate to Tom's desires, fears, and triumphs.

Another feature that makes the novel so engaging is its rich background setting and memorable characters. From Tom's loyal companion Huckleberry Finn to the kind-hearted Aunt Polly, each character is portrayed with depth and authentic regional dialogue. The exciting plot moves seamlessly from lighthearted schoolroom pranks to thrilling midnight adventures in mysterious graveyards and dark caves.

Furthermore, the book carries subtle lessons about honesty, friendship, and moral courage without ever feeling preachy. Tom's willingness to stand up for justice during critical moments shows his underlying goodness, making him a deeply endearing protagonist.

In conclusion, The Adventures of Tom Sawyer is a timeless masterpiece that offers laughter, excitement, and nostalgia in equal measure. Every time I reopen its pages, I am transported back to a world of endless imagination and joyful discovery.

4. A Wedding in the Family

Last week, our entire family gathered in Jaipur to celebrate the wedding of my elder cousin, Radhika. The venue was a magnificently decorated heritage hall adorned with marigold garlands, fairy lights, and elegant silk drapes. The air was filled with festive excitement as relatives from distant cities arrived to participate in the traditional ceremonies.

The wedding festivities spanned three memorable days, beginning with the lively Mehendi and Sangeet functions. Family members of all ages performed traditional dances and sang folk songs, creating a joyful environment. On the main wedding day, the groom arrived in a grand procession accompanied by lively brass band music and dancing guests. The central wedding ritual took place around a sacred fire under a beautifully decorated mandap, where solemn vows were recited by the couple.

What I liked most about the event was the warm sense of togetherness that brought our extended family close. Reconnecting with cousins, sharing old stories, and participating in rich cultural rituals made the occasion truly special. Additionally, the grand wedding feast—featuring a magnificent spread of traditional Rajasthani dishes and sweets—was an absolute delight for everyone present.

However, there were a few aspects of the event that I found slightly unpleasant. The continuous use of loud sound systems late into the night was exhausting, especially for senior family members. Furthermore, I observed a considerable amount of food wastage at the buffet counters, which could have been avoided with better management.

Despite these minor drawbacks, my cousin's wedding was a beautiful celebration of love, culture, and family bonds. The vibrant memories of colorful attire, joyous laughter, and solemn customs will remain etched in my heart for years to come.

5. My Favourite Extra-curricular Activities

In today's fast-paced academic environment, extra-curricular activities provide a vital outlet for creativity and self-expression. In my spare time, I love engaging in two main activities: playing classical violin and participating in school debate competitions. Both pursuits bring immense joy to my life while shaping my personality in unique ways.

Practicing the violin requires patience, discipline, and consistent effort. Learning to read musical notation and controlling the bow to produce sweet melodies demands hours of focused concentration. When I play music, I feel a sense of inner calm and emotional freedom that helps me recharge after long hours of study. Music has taught me that mastery over any skill requires steady perseverance and dedication.

On the other hand, participating in debate competitions challenges me to think critically and express my ideas with clarity and confidence. Preparing arguments on complex contemporary issues sharpens my analytical skills and encourages me to view problems from multiple perspectives. Standing on stage before a large audience has helped me overcome stage fright and develop strong public speaking skills.

Together, these extra-curricular pursuits contribute significantly to my overall character development. Music nurtures my emotional intelligence and instills patience, while debating fosters mental agility, confidence, and articulate communication. They have taught me how to balance discipline with creativity and work gracefully both individually and in team settings.

In conclusion, extra-curricular activities are essential for holistic personal growth. They enrich our school life, build essential life skills, and help us discover our true passions beyond textbooks and examinations.

writing.title: Article Writing
writing.html:
📌 What is an Article?

An article is a comprehensive piece of writing published in newspapers or school magazines. In Class IX, an article expects a mature analysis of a topic—usually a social issue, environmental concern, or a teenage-centric problem. It must present a balanced view, including causes, effects, and pragmatic solutions.

📝 Format / Structure (Word Limit: 120-150 words)

  1. Title/Heading: Centered, catchy, and relevant. (Capitalize main words).
  2. Byline: Just below the title on the right (e.g., By Amit, Class IX-A).
  3. Paragraph 1 (Introduction - The Hook):
    - Start with a striking fact, a quote, or a rhetorical question.
    - Introduce the topic and its current relevance.
  4. Paragraph 2 (Body - Analysis):
    - Causes: Why is this issue happening?
    - Effects: How does it impact society, students, or the environment?
    - Include statistics or real-life examples to strengthen your point.
  5. Paragraph 3 (Conclusion - The Solution):
    - Suggest practical, actionable solutions.
    - Conclude with a strong, thought-provoking sentence or a call to action.

⚖️ CBSE Marking Scheme (Typically 5-8 Marks)

  • Format (Title + Byline): 1 Mark
  • Content (Ideas, logic, relevance): 3-4 Marks
  • Expression (Grammatical accuracy, mature vocabulary, cohesion): 2-3 Marks

💡 Language Tips & Key Rules

  • Formal Tone: Do not use slang, abbreviations, or conversational language.
  • Linkers / Connectors: Use words like Furthermore, consequently, paradoxically, inevitably, therefore to connect your sentences smoothly.
  • Third Person Perspective: Generally, use the third person ("It is evident that..."). You can use "we" in the conclusion when calling for collective action.

⚠️ Common Mistakes to Avoid

  • Writing the article without paragraphs. It MUST be broken into Intro, Body, and Conclusion.
  • Providing problems without suggesting any solutions at the end.
  • Straying away from the given topic.

🌟 Model Example

Q: You are Rohan/Riya. Write an article for your school magazine on the topic: "The Menace of Cyberbullying Among Teenagers."

The Menace of Cyberbullying Among Teenagers
By Riya

The digital age has brought the world to our fingertips, but it has also unleashed a silent, invisible monster: cyberbullying. With the exponential rise in the use of social media among teenagers, the internet has unfortunately become a breeding ground for harassment and intimidation.

Unlike traditional bullying, cyberbullying does not stop at the school gates; it follows the victim home. Hiding behind the veil of anonymity, bullies use fake profiles to post derogatory comments, spread malicious rumors, or share embarrassing photographs. The consequences are devastating. Victims often suffer from severe anxiety, depression, and a steep decline in academic performance. In extreme cases, it leads to tragic outcomes like self-harm.

Eradicating this menace requires a collective effort. Parents and teachers must cultivate an environment where teenagers feel safe discussing their online experiences without fear of losing their internet privileges. Furthermore, schools should conduct regular awareness workshops on cyber ethics. As responsible netizens, teenagers must learn to block and report toxic behavior, ensuring the internet remains a space for learning, not torment.

✍️ Practice Prompts

  1. Write an article on "The Importance of Mental Health Awareness in Schools." Highlight how academic pressure affects students and what can be done.
  2. Write an article on "Water Scarcity: The Looming Crisis." Detail the causes and the urgent need for water conservation.

literature.html:
Let us read

I.

Word Meaning
Splashed Fell in drops, making a sound
Slithered Moved by sliding from side to side
Murmuring Speaking in a low voice
Startled Surprised
Thicket A dense group of bushes and trees
Shrieked Made a high-pitched sound

A big bright tear splashed down her nose. And another. A kingfisher swept down, its wings an arrow of blue in the sunlight. And a green lizard slithered down to the river's edge to bask in the sun.

"Dear, dear!" said a sleepy, murmuring voice, "What's the matter?"

Jahnavi was startled, because she was sure she had been quite alone. It couldn't have been the lizard. And the kingfisher was up in the thicket of bamboo eating the fish it had caught. It couldn't be the parrots, because parrots shrieked and this was such a sleepy voice. She looked around her. There wasn't a soul in sight. She was rather scared and wanted to run away.

"You shouldn't cry, you know," the voice went on. "And you really shouldn't be scared, when you have been coming here to see me every day, well, almost every day."

She was puzzled. It was such a voice, like the river. It couldn't be the river!

"Well, tell me all about it," said the River, for it was the River. "I've got to hurry to reach the sea, you know."

"They won't let me go to school," said Jahnavi. "I asked my mother, 'Why can't I go to school like Ettan and Meena?' And Mother had replied, 'You are too small, baby. Maybe later.'" But when she was five, little Ramu was born and Mother still said, "Maybe next year. Jahnavi, mind your little brother while I go to the fields." Now, she was nearly ten and minding Little Appu, who was the smallest. "They don't want me. They only..."—she stopped with a sob...

"I am scared to go to school. And I'm so old now, they'll never let me go. But I want to go. I want to learn to read like Ettan and Meena." Jahnavi called her brother 'Ettan'. Ettan means 'Elder brother', but his real name was Gopi. "I want to know why spiders are yellow in yellow flowers, why bamboo trees rustle, why the moon always comes from behind the hills, never the other way, why the baby fish in the field water become frogs, why..."

"Stop!" said the River. "You make me breathless. So many whys! I can tell you where the moon goes," the River said conspiratorially. "It goes down towards the sea. I've seen; it always takes the same way—over the mountains and down to the sea, like me!"

Word Meaning
rustle light sound made by leaves rubbing against each other
conspiratorially secretly

Let us discuss

  1. What was Jahnavi's dream? Was it important to her? Why?
  2. Do you think the river can help her in fulfilling her dream? How?

II.

Word Meaning
clump a small group of trees growing together
rattling noise made by shaking things
catamaran a kind of boat
wailed (here) complained in a loud voice
"Even little Ramu goes to school," said Jahnavi, "pity, the school isn't by the sea," said the River. "Then I could take you along, you know. But, I suppose I couldn't really. You'd get your feet wet. And that would never do! I'm afraid there's only one thing you can do."

"Can I do something?" asked Jahnavi. "Well, it's up to you," said the River. "Seems to me little girls can do as much as little boys—they swim as fast as little boys. You just slip along one morning and sit there in the school and listen to what's going on, and maybe the teacher will let you stay."

"I couldn't," gasped Jahnavi. "I couldn't! They'd scare me! They'd chase me out."

The River laughed. "You? Scared?" the River said, "when you're not afraid of the green lizard, or of the snake in the bamboo clump, (Jahnavi startled) or the big trains rattling past that bridge." "Trains are noisy; I prefer ships," said the River.

Jahnavi never knew the snake lived in the bamboo clump.

"What are ships?" she asked.

"Big boats," said the River, "so big that they can take hundreds of people, and they sail along the sea with lights that shine all night."

Jahnavi held her breath. "Will they come here?" she asked.

"I'm afraid not," said the River. "Too large, you know. Chandu's catamaran is good enough for me. Chandu can take you to see a ship, someday."

"They'd never let me!" wailed Jahnavi.

"Try going to school first," said the River. "Remember—it's up to you!"

Jahnavi gathered courage. The next day she reached the school, panting and out of breath and stood by the door listening while the teacher read out the lesson. It was a story about a prince called Ašhoka, who became a great king. Little Appu had fallen asleep on her shoulder. She crept nearer and nearer till she was in the back row, squatting with the others on the earthen floor. Little Appu made no noise and she listened.

"Where did you spring from, little girl?" asked the teacher. "And what is your name? You're new in my class."

"She's Gopi's sister, Gopi is in the next class," said one of the boys. "It's Jahnavi," said another. "So, you're Gopi's little sister? Nice lad, Gopi."

"If you really, really want to come to my school, Jahnavi," the teacher had said, "we'll talk to your father about it. Don't you worry. We'll find a way."

Jahnavi saw the teacher walking up the steps to their gate the next evening when she was lighting the lamp. She could see her father scratching his cheek the way he did when he was worried and the teacher was nodding and saying something she couldn't make out. And Mother said, "Little Jahnavi, I shall miss you when you go to school. Girls should learn as much as they want. When I was your age, I wanted to go to school, but your grandmother said 'No', but now, I am glad the teacher came to talk to your father."

And Jahnavi said, "Mother, when I grow up, I'll be a teacher and I'll go from house to house in our village and ask all the little girls to come to my school. And I'll teach them all that I'm going to learn."

And she went down the path between the fields the next morning before school began, to meet the River. "I did it!" she told the River. "I was scared, but I did it! And they're letting me go. I'm going to learn to write my name and do sums and find out why our little fishes in the rice fields turn into frogs." She heard the river's sleepy chuckle, "Come again, little girl, and I'll tell you all about the ships that sail the sea."

KAMALA NAIR

(An extract adapted from The Day the River Spoke)

OBSERVING NATURE

Look closely at the plants, trees, flowers, birds, and even the sky. Make detailed notes of what you observe, focusing on textures, movements, and how light plays with these elements. Answers – THE DAY THE RIVER SPOKE

Let us discuss

Yes, it was very important to her because she had a strong desire to learn just like her elder brother and sister, instead of only staying home to look after her younger siblings.
  2. Yes, the River helped her by giving her courage and good advice. The River told Jahnavi that girls can do as much as boys and encouraged her to quietly go to the school and listen to the teacher, which finally gave her the confidence to take the first step.

Let us think and reflect

II. Answer the following questions.

  1. The writer describes different aspects of nature in detail to create a peaceful, vivid background and to show how closely connected Jahnavi is to her surroundings. This sets a calm mood and prepares the reader for the magical moment when the river speaks to her.
  2. The River knew so much about Jahnavi because she visited the riverbank almost every day, sitting there, crying, and thinking about her life, allowing the River to observe her closely over time.
  3. We can infer that Jahnavi felt she was past the usual starting age for primary school, as she was nearly ten years old. It also suggests that schools traditionally enrolled younger children, making her feel self-conscious and doubtful about being accepted.
  4. The River laughed because Jahnavi was brave enough to stay near wild creatures like green lizards and snakes, and loud trains, yet she felt scared of friendly people at school.
  5. Jahnavi should follow the River's advice because the River gave her wise, encouraging, and practical guidance that helped her overcome her fear and take charge of her own future.
  6. The conversation makes the story appealing by introducing a magical element of personification, turning a natural feature into a wise friend and making Jahnavi's thoughts and emotions come alive through dialogue.
  7. The main message is that every child, especially girls, deserves the right to education, and with courage, self-belief, and determination, one can overcome obstacles to fulfill one's dreams.

My advice to all is to protect our green spaces so that every morning remains full of life and beauty.

literature.title: Animals, Birds, and Dr. Dolittle
literature.html:
Let us read

I.

Doctor Dolittle was sitting in his kitchen talking with the Cat's-food-Man who had come to see him with a stomach-ache.

"Why don't you give up being a people's doctor, and be an animal doctor?" asked the Cat's-food-Man.

The parrot, Polynesia, was sitting in the window looking out at the rain and singing a sailor song to herself. She stopped singing and started to listen.

Doctor," the Cat's-food-Man went on, "you know all about animals—much more than what these vets here do. That book you wrote—about cats, why, it's wonderful! I can't read or write myself—my wife, Theodosia, is a scholar, and she read your book to me. You might have been a cat yourself. You know the way they think."

When the Cat's-food-Man had gone the parrot flew off the window on to the Doctor's table and said, "That man's got sense. That's what you ought to do. Be an animal doctor. Give the silly people up—if they haven't brains enough to see you're the best doctor in the world. Take care of animals instead—they'll soon find it out. Be an animal doctor."

"Oh, there are plenty of animal doctors," said John Dolittle, putting the flowerpots outside on the windowsill to get the rain.

"Yes, there are plenty," said Polynesia. "But none of them are any good at all. Now listen, Doctor, and I'll tell you something. Did you know that animals can talk?"

Word Meaning
scholar a learned person

"I knew that parrots can talk," said the Doctor.

"Oh, we parrots can talk in two languages—people's language and bird language," said Polynesia proudly. "If I say, 'Polly wants a cracker', you understand me. But hear this: Ka-ka oi-ee, fee-fee?"

"Good Gracious!" cried the Doctor. "What does that mean?"

"That means, 'Is the porridge hot yet?'—in bird language."

"My! You don't say so!" said the Doctor. "You never talked that way to me before."

"What would have been the good?" said Polynesia, dusting some cracker crumbs off her left wing. "You wouldn't have understood me if I had."

"Tell me some more," said the Doctor, all excited; and he rushed over to the drawer and came back with a book and a pencil. "Now don't go too fast—and I'll write it down. This is interesting—very interesting—something quite new. Give me the Birds' A.B.C. first—slowly now."

So that was the way the Doctor came to know that animals had a language of their own and could talk to one another. And all that afternoon, while it was raining, Polynesia sat on the kitchen table giving him bird words to put down in the book.

At teatime, when the dog, Jip, came in, the parrot said to the Doctor, "See, he's talking to you."

"Looks to me as though he were scratching his ear," said the Doctor.

"But animals don't always speak with their mouths," said the parrot in a high voice, raising her eyebrows. "They talk with their ears, with their feet, with their tails—with everything. Sometimes they don't want to make a noise. Do you see now the way he's twitching up one side of his nose?"

Word Meaning
cracker a thin, dry biscuit usually eaten with cheese
Birds' A.B.C. (here) the language that birds speak
"What's that mean?" asked the Doctor.

"That means, 'Can't you see that it has stopped raining?'" Polynesia answered. "He is asking you a question. Dogs nearly always use their noses for asking questions."

After a while, with the parrot's help, the Doctor got to learn the language of the animals so well that he could talk to them himself and understand everything they said. Then he gave up being a people's doctor altogether.

Let us discuss

I. Complete the following sentence by selecting a suitable reason.
The Cat's-food-Man suggests to Doctor Dolittle that he should become an animal doctor because he believes that Dolittle __________________

  1. earns less fee by treating human patients
  2. enjoys the company of animals as they speak less
  3. dislikes spending time with human patients
  4. knows more about animals than the local veterinarians

    III. Do you think Doctor Dolittle would be famous as an animal doctor? If yes, why? If not, why not?

II.

As soon as the Cat's-food-Man had told everyone that John Dolittle was going to become an animal doctor, old ladies began to bring him their pet pugs and poodles who had eaten too much cake; and farmers came many miles to show him sick cows and sheep.

One day a plough horse was brought to him; and the poor thing was terribly glad to find a man who could talk in horse language.

"You know, Doctor," said the horse, "that vet over the hill knows nothing at all. He has been treating me six weeks now—for something or the other. What I need is spectacles. I am going blind in one eye. There's no reason why horses shouldn't wear glasses, the same as people. But that stupid man over the hill never even looked at my eyes. He kept on giving me big pills. I tried to tell him, but he couldn't understand a word of horse language. What I need is spectacles."

"Of course—of course," said the Doctor. "I'll get you some at once."

"I would like a pair like yours," said the horse—"only green. They'll keep the Sun out of my eyes while I'm ploughing the field."

"Certainly," said the Doctor. "Green ones you shall have."

"You know, the trouble is, Sir," said the plough horse as the Doctor opened the front door to let him out—"the trouble is that anybody thinks he can doctor animals—just because the animals don't complain. As a matter of fact, it takes a much cleverer man to be a really good animal doctor than it does to be a good people's doctor."

"Well, well!" said the Doctor.

"When will my glasses be ready?"

"I'll have them for you next week," said the Doctor.
"Come in again Tuesday—Good morning!"

Word Meaning
countryside rural area
Then John Dolittle got a fine, big pair of green spectacles; and the plough horse stopped going blind in one eye and could see as well as ever.

And soon it became a common sight to see farm animals wearing glasses in the countryside, round Puddleby; and a blind horse was a thing unknown.

And so it was with all the other animals that were brought to him. As soon as they found that he could talk their language, they told him where the pain was and how they felt, and of course it was easy for him to cure them.

Now all these animals went back and told their brothers and friends that there was a doctor in the little house with the big garden who really was a doctor. And whenever any creatures got sick—not only horses and cows and dogs—but all the little things of the fields, like harvest mice, badgers, and bats, all came at once to his house on the edge of the town, so that his big garden was nearly always crowded with animals trying to get in to see him.

There were so many that came that he had to have special doors made for the different kinds. He wrote 'HORSES' over the front door, 'COWS' over the side door, and 'SHEEP' on the kitchen door. Each kind of animal had a separate door—even the mice had a tiny tunnel made for them into the cellar, where they waited patiently in rows for the Doctor to come round to them.

And so, in a few years' time, every living thing for miles and miles got to know about John Dolittle, M.D. And the birds who flew to other countries in the winter told the animals in foreign lands about Dolittle who could understand their talk and help them in their troubles. In this way he became famous among the animals—all over the world. He was happy and liked his life very much.

HUGH LOFTING

Word Meaning

Let us read

One day a funny kind of man
Came walking down this street
He wore a shoe upon his head
And hats upon his feet.

He raised the shoe and smiled at me,
His manners were polite;
But never had I seen before
Such a funny sounding sight.

He said, 'Allow me to present
Your Highness with a rose.'
And taking out a currant bun
He held it to my nose.

I staggered back against the wall
And then I answered, 'Well!
I never saw a rose with such
A funny looking smell.'

He then began to sing a song,
And sat down on the ground;
You never heard in all your life
Such a funny feeling sound.

'My friend, why do you wear two hats
Upon your feet?' I said.
He turned the other way about,
And hopped home on his head.

NATALIE JOAN

Summary

The poem describes a bizarre and amusing encounter with a "funny kind of man" who does everything in an upside-down manner — wearing a shoe on his head and hats on his feet, offering a currant bun as a "rose," and hopping home on his head. The speaker engages with the man, finding his behavior absurd yet oddly charming. The poet uses dialogue and repetition of the word "funny" to emphasize the nonsensical, lighthearted nature of the encounter. The poem celebrates harmless silliness and the joy of unexpected humor in everyday life.

Poetic Devices

  • Repetition — The word "funny" is repeated throughout ("funny kind of man," "funny sounding sight," "funny looking smell," "funny feeling sound") to reinforce the humorous and absurd tone.

  • Alliteration — "funny feeling," "funny sounding," "funny looking" create a playful, rhythmic pattern.

  • Inversion — "Never had I seen before / Such a funny sounding sight" uses reversed word order for poetic rhythm.

  • Dialogue — The inclusion of direct speech ("Allow me to present Your Highness with a rose") makes the poem lively and conversational.

  • Humor/Irony — The contrast between the man's polite manners and his absurd actions creates situational irony.

  • Synesthesia — "Funny sounding sight," "funny looking smell," "funny feeling sound" deliberately mix sensory categories (sound+sight, sight+smell, feeling+sound), creating an absurd, disorienting effect that mirrors the man's upside-down world.

  • Oxymoron — "Funny sounding sight" combines contradictory sensory experiences, heightening the nonsense.

  • Hyperbole — The entire scenario is exaggerated beyond plausibility — a man wearing shoes on his head and hats on his feet — to maximize comedic effect.

  • Imagery — "He wore a shoe upon his head / And hats upon his feet" paints a vivid, comical visual.

Rhyme Scheme

ABCB — each stanza uses a four-line pattern with lines 2 and 4 rhyming (e.g., street/feet, me/be, rose/nose, ground/sound).

literature.title: Say the Right Thing
literature.html:
Let us read

This is a humorous play in which a mother advises her daughter to say the right thing at the right time. However, when guests arrive, the daughter hilariously forgets her mother's guidance.

Read the play to find out how she commits blunders and embarrasses the guests as well as her mother.

Character Description
MARY SHAW a young girl
MRS. SHAW Mary's mother
MRS. HARDING the wife of Mr. Harding, a wealthy man
MRS. LEE Mr. Harding's married sister
Word Meaning
hilariously in a very funny way
blunders careless mistakes
embarrasses makes (the guests) uncomfortable

Scene I

MRS. SHAW: The room looks cleaner now. Put that coat away in your bedroom. This room isn't the place for coats.

Mrs. Harding and Mrs. Lee will soon be here, and they don't want to see that.

MARY : You're always telling me to put things away.

MRS. SHAW: Yes, I am. You leave your clothes all over the house.

MARY : I'm not a child!

MRS. SHAW: No, you're not. So please keep your clothes in your own room.

MARY : Why are those two women coming here? Who's Mrs. Harding?

MRS. SHAW: She's the wife of a wealthy man, Mr. Harding. He has just bought a big house in Lanfield. They lived in London before. She's coming to have a talk. I met her in a shop and asked her to come.

MARY : Oh, I've seen her children. They often come along the road. Who's Mrs. Lee?

MRS. SHAW: She's Mr. Harding's sister. She has been staying with them for a while.

MARY : What are you going to talk about?

MRS. SHAW: I don't know. All kinds of things. One day you'll have to go to some of these houses yourself and talk to the people there.

MARY : I can talk now. I've been able to talk for a long time.

MRS. SHAW: Yes, that's true. You always talk too much. But does anyone want to hear the things that you say?

MARY : I can talk very well when I like. I'll stay with you today and talk to them when they come.

MRS. SHAW: Oh, I don't think so. You can go out for a walk. It will be better if you do that.

MARY : Why?

MRS. SHAW: If you stay with me, you may not say the right thing.

MARY : I know the right things to say: 'Good afternoon', 'How are you?' and things like that. Let me stay today. I can do it very well. I'll show you. Anyone can talk.

MRS. SHAW: You may stay if you like. But take care. I want to know Mrs. Harding well. I want her to ask me to go to their house. There isn't much to do here in Lanfield, and I want to know some more people. I want some more friends here. So take care when you say anything.

MARY : Tell me what to say.

MRS. SHAW: I can't tell you everything, but you'll always be right if you're kind to people. Say things that will please them. Then they'll like you. Laugh a lot, and try to make them laugh too. And if everyone stops talking, say something to make them talk again. They don't want to sit here and look at the floor without speaking. Think of something to say.

MARY : I can do that. There's always something to say. Must I do anything else?

MRS. SHAW: When they are ready to leave, don't jump out of your chair and look gladly at the door. You must look sorry when they want to leave.

MARY : What shall I do when they want to go?

MRS. SHAW: Ask them to stay a little while longer. Just say, 'Must you go? Can't you stay?' or something like that. You like them and you want them to stay, and you must let them understand that.

MARY : That's not very hard, is it? I'll remember that. 'Must you go? Can't you stay? Must you go? Can't you stay?'

MRS. SHAW: That's right. Now take your coat to your room and change into a clean dress. You must look nice when they come. And if everyone stops talking, say something kind to make them talk again. And don't say anything that will make them angry.

MARY : I will remember. I've often done harder things than this.

Speaker Words of the Speaker Reason

I'm not a child!

II. Do you think Mary will be able to follow her mother's advice successfully when Mrs. Harding and Mrs. Lee visit? Why or why not?

Scene II

MRS. SHAW : So you like Lanfield, Mrs. Harding! I'm very glad.

MRS. HARDING : Yes, we like it very much. It's not the same as London, but there are some very nice people here, and we've found a good house. (No one says anything more, and Mrs. Shaw looks at Mary.)

MARY : What beautiful children you have, Mrs. Harding! I've often seen them walking along the road.

MRS. HARDING : Oh, I haven't any children.

MARY : Oh, yes, you have! I've seen them: a little boy and a little girl.

MRS. HARDING : (not very pleased) I have no children; believe me.

MARY : Oh!

MRS. SHAW : (quietly) They must be someone else's children. Have you met Mr. Best? He's a nice man. He lives near you.

MARY : Oh, Mr. Best! He lives here and he works in London. He goes all the way to London by train every morning, and then he comes all the way back by train every night. He lives in trains! (she laughs) What kind of life is that? Why do people do things like that? They do not know how to live. And he reads two newspapers in the train every day. He never reads a book. But he's only a banker, and bankers can't think.

MRS. LEE : My brother's a banker. He goes to London by train every morning and comes back every night. He reads two newspapers in the train in the morning, and another every night.

MARY : Oh, I'm sorry. I didn't know.

MRS. SHAW : Bankers always have to read a lot of newspapers. Do you know Mrs. Best? She's a nice woman. I like her.

MARY : But have you seen her clothes? She goes out in a blue dress with a red coat over it. (she laughs)

MRS. HARDING: I have a blue dress, and I often put on my red coat at the same time.

MRS. SHAW: (quickly) I like blue dresses and red coats. (No one says anything.)

MARY: I saw Mrs. Cotter this afternoon. I met her in the street. No one sees her in the morning because she always stays in bed then. And she's always asking the doctor to go to see her. I can't understand women who stay in bed in the morning. And why must she always ask for the doctor? I've never been to a doctor in my life.

MRS. HARDING: I stay in bed in the morning myself.

MRS. LEE: I often go to the doctor.

MARY: Oh, I'm sorry. (No one speaks.)

MRS. SHAW: Do you know Mrs. Grantley? She's one of my best friends.

MARY: But she's so talkative! Talkative women aren't very interesting, are they?

MRS. LEE: My mother's a very talkative woman.

MARY: Oh, I'm sorry. I didn't know. (No one says anything.)

MARY: (looking out of the window): Oh, there's that dog again! It always looks very dirty. I don't like dogs, do you? Who wants a dog? That dog's always near our house. Why do people keep dogs? Who wants a dog? Why doesn't its owner keep it clean? Have you seen it?

MRS. HARDING: (looking out of the window) Yes, I've seen it. That's Towzer. It's our dog.

MARY : (with a red face) Oh, I didn't know! (No one speaks.)

MARY : (still looking out of the window) There's Mr. Pomeroy on his horse. He's always talking about horses. He rides a horse every day, and practises shooting. Why must he do that? What have they done to Mr. Pomeroy? Why do some men like horses more than they like people? It's hard to understand men.

MRS. LEE : My brother practises shooting when he has the time, and he rides his horse when he can. He sold his house in London and bought a house here because he wanted to ride and practise shooting.

MRS. HARDING : (looking at Mrs. Lee) It's getting a little late. We must go now, Mrs. Shaw. It has been very nice to have a little talk. (She looks at Mary.)

MRS. LEE : Very nice. (She looks at Mary.)

MRS. SHAW : It was very good of you to come to see us. Please stay a little longer.

MARY : (unable to say the right thing even now) Oh, must you stay? Can't you go?

G.C. THORNLEY

Say the Right Thing

In the quiet town of Lanfield, Mrs. Shaw was tidying her living room in preparation for a visit from Mrs. Harding, the wife of a wealthy local man, and her sister-in-law, Mrs. Lee. Mrs. Shaw wanted to make a good impression and make new friends. Her young daughter, Mary, wanted to stay and meet the guests. Although Mrs. Shaw advised Mary to go for a walk because she feared Mary might say the wrong things, Mary insisted she was fully capable of polite conversation. Mrs. Shaw gave her final advice: be kind, say pleasing things, and fill awkward silences.

When the guests arrived, Mary immediately began attempting conversation, but every attempt turned into a hilarious blunder. First, Mary complimented Mrs. Harding on her "beautiful children," only to be told firmly that Mrs. Harding had no children at all. Next, Mary mocked Mr. Best for commuting on trains and reading newspapers, calling bankers unthinking people—only for Mrs. Lee to reveal that her own brother was a banker who did the exact same thing.

Mary's blunders continued without pause. She made fun of Mrs. Best's combination of a blue dress and red coat, only to learn Mrs. Harding wore the exact same outfit. She criticized women who stay in bed in the morning and call doctors, only to have Mrs. Harding state that she stayed in bed in the morning and Mrs. Lee add that she visited the doctor often. She complained about talkative women, dirty dogs, and men who ride horses, only to discover each remark insulted Mrs. Lee's mother, Mrs. Harding's dog Towzer, and Mrs. Lee's brother respectively. Each blunder was met with awkward silence and Mary's face growing redder.

Finally, when the uncomfortable guests rose to leave, Mrs. Shaw politely asked them to stay longer. Mary tried to repeat her mother's coached farewell phrase, but mixed up her words completely, asking, "Must you stay? Can't you go?" The visit ended in utter awkwardness, proving that confidence without tact and thinking before speaking can turn any polite conversation into a disaster.

literature.html:
Let us read

Word Meaning
racket a loud and disturbing noise
sopping soaking
scowling having an angry or frowning expression
rigged up assembled something temporarily
tinkering experimenting or fiddling
dynamos electric generator

I.

"Who put that water bag here?" roared my father from the front doorstep. "Your burglar alarm," I hissed to my brother Anand, who was getting ready to disappear from the house. Ma rushed in to see what the racket was all about and found Papa standing there, sopping wet and scowling.

"I want to know who is behind this nonsense," Papa said grimly.

"I think it's supposed to be a burglar alarm," Ma said, in a soothing voice.

"I don't care what it's supposed to be," Papa said.

"Where's that boy? I'm sure he rigged this up."

Anand had vanished by this time and reappeared only after dinner when Papa had cooled down.

Before this story, let me put you in the picture. I am Anita, fourteen years old. My brother Anand, one year younger than me, caused all that hoo-ha with his burglar alarm.

And this is not the first time he's got on Papa's nerves or frightened someone half to death in the house. The trouble with him is that he thinks he is a scientist. He loves tinkering with all sorts of electrical gadgets, tools, dynamos, planks of wood, and things like that. And he keeps creating 'inventions' that never work out as they are supposed to.

Recently there had been a rush of thefts in the colony and Anand had got it into his head that what was needed was a burglar alarm. So, the minute Papa left for the office and Ma for the market, he started on his latest scheme. As usual I had to be involved, though I'd have preferred to finish my novel. "If you get a shelling, don't bring me in," I warned Anand.

"Nothing will go wrong this time. I've planned it out carefully. See the blueprint."

Anand loves words like blueprint—it makes him feel professional! Anyway, I looked at the elaborate drawing of doors, wires, and bells and asked, "How does this thing work?"

"It's quite simple. The moment the door opens, this alarm is tripped off and makes a clanging sound. Then this water bag here is loosened and falls on the thief's head. By then we call the police—simple!"

"But how does the alarm know that a burglar is opening the door?"

"I've taken care of that," Anand said loftily. I had my own doubts about the alarm's guessing powers, but kept them to myself because when Anand is in one of his inventive moods, nothing stops him.

"You see," Anand explained smugly, "A thief tries to open the door stealthily. I've rigged it up so that the alarm works only when the door is opened gently."

I was sceptical. "Remember, if Papa asks, I'm not involved," I warned. "Now clean up this mess before anyone gets home."

As you already know, my doubts about the alarm were quite justified. Papa, who always opens the door softly, was thoroughly soaked and angry as angry could be. Anyway, for a week after this, Anand did not dare try out anything new. Then we saw this film 'Back to the Future'. I don't know if you have seen it, but it's all about a time machine. Well, that was

the end of peace and quiet in the house.

My brother decided that he had to make a time machine too. Papa locked up his tool box and hid the key while Ma kept a wary eye on her oven and mixer. Because, as I told you, when Anand is on one of his inventing binges, he takes apart all the gadgets in the house to collect parts. You can't imagine the noise that

Word Meaning
elaborate detailed
clanging a loud ringing sound like that of a metal being hit
smugly proudly
stealthily quietly or carefully so that one is not seen or heard
sceptical doubtful
frantic hurried and disorganised
crestfallen look sad and disappointed appearance
offended felt upset or hurt

was going on—hammering and sawing and clattering. Anand's room, next to our room, was transformed into a network of wires, springs, levers, and bulbs. There was an enormous panel which was to be control switchboard. As for Anand, he went around looking like a savage. When Ma didn't notice, the fellow didn't even comb his hair.

Anand just wouldn't let anyone into his room. Finally, after a fortnight of frantic activity, the time machine was ready. "We can try it out tonight," Anand announced to everyone at home at lunch time.

"I don't know what you've been up to in that room, but you're not trying out anything new," Papa said firmly.

"But it's a time machine! I've invented it," Anand protested.

"When I say NO, I mean NO," Papa said, glaring.

"Poor boy," Ma said noticing Anand's crestfallen look.

"At least let's take a look at it."

Papa sighed. "All right, but if the house falls, it's your fault."

As it turned out, we could not try out the time machine that day at all. The next day, Papa and Ma were going to Kharagpur, a few hours away from Calcutta (now Kolkata), for a wedding. Ma was worried about leaving us alone, but we reassured her. "We're old enough to look after ourselves, Ma," I said. "And we can go next door to Sharma Aunty if we need anything."

"And it's only one night," Anand added.

"All right. But promise me you won't do anything with that time machine till we come back," Ma said sternly, looking at Anand. He promised half-heartedly, offended at this lack of respect for his creation. I breathed a sigh of relief.

I. Complete the cause-and-effect table given below.

Causes Effects
1. Anand set up his burglar alarm and rigged it to work when the door was opened softly.
2. Anita was able to avoid any responsibility as Anand faced the consequences alone.

4. Papa firmly said 'NO' to trying out the time machine.

II.

They left by the afternoon train and were coming back the following evening. Anand fell asleep immediately, but I stayed up to finish a novel. At about eleven thirty I thought I heard a scratching at the front door. Telling myself it was only my imagination, I went back to the book. A little later there was a rattle and a click. I was really scared, I can tell you, what with a murder story before me and then strange noises in the middle of the night! I shook Anand and whispered, 'Listen, there's someone at the door.'

'Go and open it then,' he muttered groggily.

'You silly! Someone's trying to get in,' I said.

Anand sat up. 'Who? What?'

'I don't know,' I said. 'What shall we do?'

'Let's holler for help,' he said. Before we could do anything, the door swung open and we found ourselves looking at a ruffianly fellow with a green scarf around his neck. Anand gasped.

'Hey, it's Boppa!' I whispered. It was indeed the fellow who had recently begun sweeping out the compounds in our row of houses. So, he was the thief, and no wonder. He knew exactly when the occupants were out, leaving the coast clear.

The fellow gave an evil grin. 'One squeak out of you and see what happens,' he said, brandishing his cudgel and backing out of the room. We heard him slide the latch in.

'What do we do now?' I asked in a low voice.

Word Meaning

ruffianly rough or violent looking
gasped took a short, deep breath in surprise
brandishing waving
cudgel a short, thick stick used as a weapon
"Let's shout anyway," Anand suggested.

The door opened suddenly again in the middle of our discussion.

"No noise from you! Now, where is your father's room?"

I was about to direct him upstairs when Anand said quickly, "The one next to this one."

"You silly goose!" I said angrily as soon as the man had gone.

"That's your room. He'll come back as mad as mad can be."

"At least it will give us some time to think of something," Anand said. "He'll take a while to locate the light switch. Let's shout." All of a sudden there was a crash followed by a loud scream. More strange noises emerged from the next room—a few muffled thumps, an eerie whine, and a low, humming sound.

"My time machine, he's started it!" Anand gasped. "I wish we could get out of this room and see what is happening out there."

There was another howl, much fainter this time, and a great deal of clattering. We shouted for all we were worth. In a few minutes, we heard footsteps running up our drive. Thankfully we recognised Mrs. Sharma's voice, along with her husband and Dr. Mohan—also a neighbour.

"Anand! Anita! Children, what's the matter? Where are you?"

Word Meaning

eerie strange
clattering continuous loud noises

"Here!" we shouted in unison. In a minute the door was unlocked.

"What on earth has been happening here, children?" Sharma Uncle asked. Both Anand and I fell over ourselves trying to explain. "Where is the fellow now?"

"The last we heard, he was in the time machine," I explained hastily, seeing everyone looking rather puzzled.

Word Meaning
unison together
hastily quickly

We entered the room cautiously and turned on the lights. The time machine was still humming softly but otherwise there was no other sound from the room.

"Well, where is he?" Dr. Mohan asked, peering behind the door. "Did you imagine this?"

"Oh no," I protested. "How could both of us have imagined the same thing?"

"Maybe he ran out," Anand suggested.

"I'm sure we'd have seen him. There's only one way out of this house and we came the same way as soon as we heard you," Sharma Uncle sounded very sure.

"Look!" Anand said, pointing to the floor. "He was wearing that." Near the panel of switches was the green scarf.

Word Meaning

indulgently fondly
intruders people who enter a place without permission
dismantled taken apart
